core.p: Without a commutator, the coil would turn half a rotation and then rock back and stop, because the forces would push it back the other way. The **split-ring commutator** fixes this.
bullets: The commutator is a ring split into two halves, fixed to the coil and rotating with it.
Carbon **brushes** press against the commutator to connect the coil to the supply while it spins.
Every **half turn** (when the coil is perpendicular to the field) the halves swap brushes, so the **current in the coil reverses**.
This means the side of the coil on the left always has current in the same direction, so the force on it is always the same way and the coil keeps turning in **one direction**.
The brushes are made of carbon (graphite) because it conducts and is slippery, so there is little friction.

callouts.p: A device that reverses the direction of the current in the coil every half turn, so the motor keeps rotating in the same direction.

core.h: Making a motor faster, stronger or reversed
core.p: Because the turning effect comes from the forces on the coil sides, anything that increases F = BIl on each side increases the turning effect.
bullets: Increase the **current** (higher supply p.d.).
Use a **stronger magnet** (larger B).
Use **more turns** of wire on the coil: each turn adds its force.
Use a **larger coil** (longer sides in the field).
Put the coil on a **soft iron core** (armature) to strengthen the field through it.
To **reverse** the direction of rotation: reverse the current **or** swap the magnetic poles.

core.p: A motor transfers energy **electrically** from the supply to a **kinetic store** of the coil and its load.
bullets: Some energy is dissipated by heating in the coil resistance and by friction at the brushes and bearings.
Efficiency = useful output energy / total input energy.
Real motors use curved pole pieces and many coils at different angles to give a smooth, steady turning effect.

core.p: The motor effect turns electrical energy into movement in many everyday devices.
bullets: Electric motors in fans, drills, washing machines, electric cars and lifts.
Loudspeakers and headphones (a coil vibrates instead of rotating).
Moving-coil meters (older ammeters) where the force turns a pointer against a spring.

analogy.t: Turning a steering wheel with two hands
analogy.p: Steering a car, you push one hand up and pull the other down on opposite sides of the wheel. The two forces are opposite, but because they act on opposite sides of the centre they make the wheel turn, just like the opposite forces on the two sides of a motor coil. To keep the wheel spinning round and round you would have to swap which hand pushes up every half turn: that is the job of the split-ring commutator. The analogy breaks down because your hands are pushed by muscles, while the coil's forces come from the interaction of two magnetic fields and exist only while the current flows.

terms.d: The force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field, caused by the interaction of the two fields.
First finger = field, second finger = current, thumb = motion (force), all at right angles on the left hand.
A measure of the strength of a magnetic field, in tesla (T).
The unit of flux density: 1 T gives a force of 1 N on 1 m of wire carrying 1 A at right angles to the field.
Force (N) = magnetic flux density (T) x current (A) x length (m), for a wire at right angles to the field.
Current direction from the positive terminal to the negative terminal.
At right angles (90 degrees); the arrangement that gives maximum force.
A field with the same strength and direction everywhere.
Many turns of insulated wire; more turns increase the turning effect in a motor.
A split ring that reverses the current in a motor coil every half turn so it keeps turning one way.
Carbon contacts that press on the commutator to connect the rotating coil to the supply.
The rotating effect of a force about a pivot; in a motor produced by opposite forces on the coil sides.
The rotating coil (often on a soft iron core) in a motor.
The combined field of a magnet and a current-carrying wire, strong on one side and weak on the other.

mistakes.w: Use the right hand for the motor effect.
mistakes.r: Use Fleming's LEFT-hand rule for the force on a current-carrying wire.

mistakes.w: The thumb shows the current.
mistakes.r: First finger = field, second finger = current, thumb = force (motion).

mistakes.w: The force is biggest when the wire is parallel to the field.
mistakes.r: The force is maximum when the wire is perpendicular to the field and zero when parallel.

mistakes.w: Calculating F = BIl with l = 5 cm gives F = 0.2 x 3 x 5 = 3 N.
mistakes.r: Convert length to metres: l = 0.05 m, so F = 0.2 x 3 x 0.05 = 0.03 N.

mistakes.w: The commutator changes a.c. to d.c. for the motor.
mistakes.r: The split-ring commutator reverses the current in the coil every half turn so the coil keeps turning the same way.

mistakes.w: Reversing both the current and the magnet reverses the motor.
mistakes.r: Reversing both cancels out; the motor turns the same way. Reverse only one of them.

mistakes.w: The forces on both sides of the coil are in the same direction, so it moves.
mistakes.r: The forces on the two sides are in opposite directions, producing a turning effect.

mistakes.w: Field lines go from S to N when using the rule.
mistakes.r: The field direction (first finger) is from N to S.

mistakes.w: Making the coil turn faster: use a bigger battery so the voltage is higher only.
mistakes.r: Any of: larger current, stronger magnet, more turns, larger coil area; name the physics quantity.

exam.q: State what is meant by the motor effect.
model: A force acts on a current-carrying wire (conductor) placed in a magnetic field.
exam.tip: Include all three ideas: current, field, force.

exam.q: State the three quantities represented by the fingers in Fleming's left-hand rule.
model: First finger: magnetic field (N to S).
Second finger: current; thumb: force (motion). (Both needed for second mark)
exam.tip: Match each finger to its quantity; do not just list the words.

exam.q: A wire 0.05 m long carries a current of 3.0 A at right angles to a magnetic field of flux density 0.20 T. Calculate the force on the wire.
exam.tip: Show the substitution even when it is easy.

exam.q: A force of 0.012 N acts on a 4.0 cm length of wire carrying 2.0 A at right angles to a field. Calculate the magnetic flux density.
exam.tip: A mark is often given for converting cm to m.

exam.q: State two ways of increasing the force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field.
model: Increase the current.
Use a stronger magnet (greater flux density) or a longer length of wire in the field.
exam.tip: Turning the wire to be perpendicular also counts if it was not already.

exam.q: A wire is placed parallel to the field lines between two magnets. Explain why there is no force on it.
model: The motor effect force needs the current to have a component at right angles to the field.
When the wire is parallel to the field there is no interaction producing a force (F = 0).
exam.tip: State the angle condition clearly.

exam.q: State two ways of reversing the direction of rotation of a d.c. motor.
model: Reverse the direction of the current (swap the battery connections).
Reverse the magnetic field (swap the poles of the magnet).
exam.tip: Doing both at once does not count.

exam.q: Explain the purpose of the split-ring commutator in a d.c. motor.
model: It reverses the direction of the current in the coil every half turn.
So the forces on each side of the coil reverse at the right moment.
So the coil keeps rotating in the same direction (instead of rocking back).
exam.tip: Every half turn is the detail examiners look for.

exam.q: Explain how a simple d.c. motor works.
model: Current flows through the coil, which is in the magnetic field of a permanent magnet.
Current flows in opposite directions along the two sides of the coil that are at right angles to the field.
By the motor effect, forces act on these sides (direction from Fleming's left-hand rule).
The forces are in opposite directions so they produce a turning effect (moment) and the coil rotates.
The split-ring commutator reverses the current in the coil every half turn.
So the forces keep turning the coil in the same direction; brushes keep contact with the rotating commutator.
exam.tip: Level of response: link current, field, force, rotation and commutator in a logical order.

exam.q: Explain why the force on the sides of the coil parallel to the field is zero.
model: The current in those sides is parallel to the magnetic field, so there is no motor effect force.
exam.tip: Short answer, use the word parallel.

exam.q: A student doubles the current and halves the length of wire in the field. Describe the effect on the force.
model: Doubling current doubles the force; halving length halves the force.
Overall the force stays the same.
exam.tip: Treat each change as a multiplier: x2 then x0.5.

worked.q: A 25 cm length of wire in a motor carries a current of 400 mA at right angles to a field of 50 mT. Calculate the force on the wire.
steps: Write the equation: F = BIl.
Convert units: B = 50 mT = 0.050 T; I = 400 mA = 0.40 A; l = 25 cm = 0.25 m.
Substitute: F = 0.050 x 0.40 x 0.25.
Calculate: F = 0.0050 N.

worked.q: A wire carries current into the page and lies in a field running from left to right (N on the left). Find the direction of the force.
steps: First finger (field): point it to the right, from N to S.
Second finger (current): point it into the page, away from you.
Your thumb now points down the page.
So the force on the wire is downwards, at right angles to both field and current.
Check: if the current were reversed (out of the page) the force would be upwards.
worked.ans: The force is downwards (towards the bottom of the page).

worked.q: A motor coil has 50 turns. Each side in the field is 0.04 m long, the current is 1.5 A and B = 0.3 T. Calculate the total force on one side of the coil.
steps: Force on one wire: F = BIl = 0.3 x 1.5 x 0.04 = 0.018 N.
Each of the 50 turns adds a wire on that side, all carrying the same current in the same direction.
Total force = 50 x 0.018 = 0.9 N.
This is why adding turns increases the turning effect of a motor.
worked.ans: 0.9 N on each side (in opposite directions on the two sides).

phy_ocrb.2.11.summary: **Electromagnetic induction** is the opposite of the motor effect: when a conductor **cuts magnetic field lines**, or the **magnetic field through a coil changes**, a **potential difference is induced** across it, and if the circuit is complete an **induced current** flows. The induced p.d. is bigger for **faster movement, a stronger field and more turns**, and it reverses if the movement or the field reverses. This effect is used in the **moving-coil microphone** (sound to electrical signal) and in generators: the **alternator** uses slip rings to give a.c. and the **dynamo** uses a split-ring commutator to give d.c. (triple).

core.p: If a wire **moves through a magnetic field** so that it **cuts field lines**, or if the **magnetic field through a coil changes**, a **potential difference (p.d.) is induced** across the ends of the wire. If the wire is part of a complete circuit, the induced p.d. drives an **induced current**.
bullets: Movement can be of the wire, of the magnet, or a change in the strength of the field (for example switching an electromagnet on or off).
**No relative movement (or no change in field) means no induced p.d.**, even in a very strong field.
A wire moving **parallel** to the field lines does not cut them, so no p.d. is induced.
This is called the **generator effect**: kinetic energy is transferred to electrical energy.

callouts.p: A potential difference is induced across a conductor when it moves relative to a magnetic field (cuts field lines) or when the magnetic field through it changes.
Induction needs change: moving or changing. A magnet resting inside a coil induces nothing.

core.h: Demonstrating induction with a magnet and coil
core.p: Connect a coil to a **sensitive centre-zero meter** (galvanometer). Move a bar magnet into and out of the coil and watch the needle.
bullets: Push the N pole **in**: the needle **deflects** one way.
Hold the magnet **still** inside: the reading is **zero**.
Pull the magnet **out**: the needle deflects the **opposite way**.
Push the **S pole** in: deflection is opposite to pushing the N pole in.
Move the magnet **faster**: a **bigger** deflection.
Keep the magnet still and move the coil instead: the same effects, because it is **relative movement** that matters.
A straight wire moved up and down between the poles of a horseshoe magnet shows the same effect on a smaller scale.

fig.cap: Pushing the N pole of a magnet into a coil changes the magnetic field through the coil, so a p.d. is induced and the centre-zero meter deflects. The induced current makes the near end of the coil a N pole, which repels the incoming magnet: the induced current opposes the change. Pulling the magnet out deflects the meter the other way; holding it still gives no reading.

core.h: Factors that affect the size of the induced p.d.
core.p: The induced p.d. depends on how quickly the magnetic field through the conductor changes, or how quickly field lines are cut.
bullets: **Speed** of movement: faster relative motion gives a bigger p.d.
**Strength of the magnetic field**: a stronger magnet gives a bigger p.d.
**Number of turns** on the coil: more turns gives a bigger p.d. (each turn adds its own p.d.).
**Area of the coil**: a larger coil links more field lines, giving a bigger p.d.
An **iron core** in the coil concentrates the field and increases the p.d.

callouts.p: All the factors come down to one idea: the faster field lines are cut (the faster the field through the coil changes), the bigger the induced p.d.

core.h: Factors that affect the direction of the induced p.d.
core.p: The direction of the induced p.d., and so of any induced current, depends on the direction of the change.
bullets: Reversing the **direction of movement** (in instead of out) reverses the p.d.
Reversing the **magnetic field** (using the other pole) reverses the p.d.
Reversing both at once gives the original direction again.
A magnet moving back and forth in a coil induces an **alternating** p.d.

core.h: The induced current opposes the change
core.p: When an induced current flows, it produces its **own magnetic field**. That field always **opposes the change** that caused it. This is consistent with conservation of energy.
bullets: Pushing a N pole into a coil makes the near end of the coil a **N pole**, which **repels** the magnet.
Pulling the N pole out makes the near end an **S pole**, which **attracts** the magnet back.
So you must do **work** to move the magnet: that work is the energy transferred to the circuit.
If the induced current helped the motion, you would get energy for nothing, which is impossible.

callouts.p: The force needed to push against the induced current's field is why turning a generator gets harder when it supplies a larger current.

core.p: A **moving-coil microphone** turns **sound waves** into an **electrical signal** using electromagnetic induction. It is built like a loudspeaker but works the other way round.
bullets: Sound waves (pressure variations) hit a thin, light **diaphragm** and make it **vibrate**.
A **coil** is attached to the diaphragm and sits in the field of a **permanent magnet**.
As the coil vibrates, it **moves relative to the magnetic field**, so it cuts field lines.
An **alternating p.d. is induced** across the coil.
The induced p.d. has the **same frequency** as the sound and its size follows the **amplitude** of the sound (louder sound, bigger p.d.).
The signal is then amplified and can be recorded, transmitted or played through a loudspeaker.

callouts.p: A microphone works by induction (movement produces p.d.), not by the motor effect (current produces force).

fig.cap: Moving-coil microphone. Sound waves make the light diaphragm vibrate. The coil fixed to it moves back and forth in the field of the permanent magnet, so the coil cuts field lines and an alternating p.d. is induced across the output leads. The p.d. has the same frequency and pattern as the sound.

core.h: Generators: rotating a coil in a field (triple)
core.p: In a generator, a coil of wire is **rotated** in a magnetic field (or a magnet is rotated inside a coil). The coil sides keep cutting field lines, so a p.d. is induced continuously.
bullets: Kinetic energy (from a turbine, engine or wheel) is transferred to electrical energy.
The induced p.d. is **greatest** when the coil's plane is **parallel** to the field: the sides are moving at right angles to the field lines and cut them **fastest**.
The induced p.d. is **zero** when the coil is **perpendicular** to the field: the sides move parallel to the field lines for an instant and cut none.
As the coil turns, each side moves up through the field and then down, so the induced p.d. **reverses every half turn**.

core.h: The alternator: a.c. with slip rings (triple)
core.p: An **alternator** generates **alternating current (a.c.)**. Each end of the rotating coil is connected to its own **slip ring**, and **brushes** press against the rings to connect the coil to the outside circuit.
bullets: The slip rings keep each end of the coil **always connected to the same brush**.
Because the induced p.d. in the coil reverses every half turn, the output p.d. also reverses: it is **alternating**.
A graph of p.d. against time is a smooth wave that goes positive then negative.
One complete turn of the coil gives **one complete cycle** of a.c.
Power-station generators and car alternators work this way (often with the magnet rotating inside fixed coils).

callouts.p: A generator that produces alternating current, using slip rings to connect the rotating coil to the circuit.

fig.cap: A simple alternator. The coil is turned in the field between the magnets. Each end of the coil is joined to its own slip ring, and carbon brushes press on the rings to take the current out to the lamp. As the coil turns, the induced p.d. reverses every half turn, so the output is alternating current.

core.h: The dynamo: d.c. with a split-ring commutator (triple)
core.p: A **dynamo** generates **direct current (d.c.)**. It uses a **split-ring commutator** instead of slip rings.
bullets: The commutator **swaps the connections** between the coil and the brushes every half turn.
It swaps them exactly when the induced p.d. in the coil reverses (coil perpendicular to the field).
So the output p.d. is **always in the same direction**: it is d.c.
The output still **varies** from zero to a maximum, so the graph is a series of humps, all on the same side of the time axis.
Bicycle dynamos and older car generators are examples.

fig.cap: Output p.d. against time. Left: an alternator (slip rings) gives alternating p.d. that is positive for half a turn and negative for the next half. Right: a dynamo (split-ring commutator) reverses the connections every half turn, so the output is always in the same direction: a varying direct p.d. Each peak happens when the coil sides cut the field lines fastest.

core.h: Reading and changing generator output graphs (triple)
core.p: Exam questions often show a p.d.-time graph and ask what it would look like after a change.
bullets: **Turn faster**: the peaks get **higher** (bigger p.d., because lines are cut faster) **and** closer together (**higher frequency**, shorter period).
**Stronger magnet or more turns**: peaks get higher, but the frequency is unchanged.
**Reverse the rotation**: the graph is inverted (positive becomes negative first).
Frequency = number of complete turns per second; period T = 1 / f.
For a dynamo, the time between humps is half the time for one rotation.

callouts.p: Turning faster changes both the amplitude and the frequency. Many students only mention one.

core.p: Electromagnetic induction is at the heart of how we generate and use electricity.
bullets: Power stations: turbines turn huge alternators.
Wind turbines and hydroelectric generators.
Bicycle dynamos, microphones, and electric guitar pick-ups.
Transformers use a changing field from an alternating current to induce a p.d. in a second coil (covered separately).

analogy.p: Think of field lines as strings stretched across a room and a wire as a stick you sweep through them. Only when the stick moves across the strings, plucking them, does it make a signal; the faster you sweep and the more strings there are (stronger field), the bigger the signal, and sweeping back the other way reverses it. Holding the stick still among the strings does nothing. The analogy breaks down because field lines are not real objects and do not get used up or pushed aside: the p.d. comes from the changing magnetic field acting on the free electrons in the wire.

terms.d: Inducing a p.d. across a conductor by moving it relative to a magnetic field or changing the field through it.
The p.d. produced across a conductor by electromagnetic induction.
The current that flows when an induced p.d. acts in a complete circuit.
Another name for electromagnetic induction used to transfer kinetic energy to electrical energy.
A sensitive meter whose needle can deflect either way, showing the direction of a small current.
A conductor moving across (not along) magnetic field lines.
A device in which sound vibrates a diaphragm and coil in a magnetic field, inducing an alternating p.d.
A thin, light sheet in a microphone that vibrates when sound waves hit it.
Current that repeatedly reverses direction.
Current that flows in one direction only.
A generator producing a.c., using slip rings.
A generator producing d.c., using a split-ring commutator.
Two complete rings, one for each end of the coil, that keep the coil connected to the same brushes.
A split ring that reverses the coil's connections every half turn so the output is d.c.
Carbon contacts pressing on the rings to connect the rotating coil to the external circuit.
Number of complete cycles per second, in hertz (Hz); equal to the number of rotations per second for an alternator.

mistakes.w: A magnet held still in a coil induces a current.
mistakes.r: There must be relative movement or a change in the field; a stationary magnet induces nothing.

mistakes.w: A current is induced whenever there is a magnetic field.
mistakes.r: A p.d. is induced only when the conductor cuts field lines or the field through it changes.

mistakes.w: Turning the generator faster only increases the voltage.
mistakes.r: It increases the peak p.d. and also increases the frequency (peaks closer together).

mistakes.w: An alternator uses a split-ring commutator.
mistakes.r: An alternator uses slip rings (a.c.); a dynamo uses a split-ring commutator (d.c.).

mistakes.w: The p.d. is largest when the coil is perpendicular to the field.
mistakes.r: The p.d. is largest when the coil plane is parallel to the field, because the sides cut the field lines fastest; it is zero when perpendicular.

mistakes.w: A microphone works by the motor effect.
mistakes.r: A microphone works by electromagnetic induction; a loudspeaker uses the motor effect.

mistakes.w: The dynamo's output is a steady d.c. like a battery.
mistakes.r: The output is in one direction but varies in size from zero to a maximum.

mistakes.w: Using a bigger magnet increases the frequency.
mistakes.r: A stronger field increases the size of the p.d. only; frequency depends on the speed of rotation.

mistakes.w: The induced current helps the magnet move into the coil.
mistakes.r: The induced current's field opposes the change, so it repels the incoming magnet.

exam.q: State what is meant by electromagnetic induction.
model: A p.d. is induced across a conductor when it moves relative to a magnetic field (or the field through it changes).
exam.tip: Mention both p.d. and movement or change.

exam.q: A magnet is held at rest inside a coil connected to a meter. State and explain the reading on the meter.
model: Zero.
There is no relative movement (no change in the magnetic field through the coil), so no p.d. is induced.
exam.tip: Explain using change, not just no movement of the meter.

exam.q: State three ways to increase the p.d. induced when a magnet is moved into a coil.
model: Move the magnet faster.
Use a stronger magnet.
Use a coil with more turns.
exam.tip: Iron core or larger coil area are also acceptable alternatives.

exam.q: State two ways of reversing the direction of the induced current.
model: Move the magnet in the opposite direction (out instead of in).
Use the opposite pole of the magnet.
exam.tip: Changing both cancels out and scores nothing.

exam.q: Explain how a moving-coil microphone produces an electrical signal from sound.
model: Sound waves make the diaphragm vibrate.
The coil attached to the diaphragm moves in the magnetic field of the permanent magnet.
The coil cuts field lines so an (alternating) p.d. is induced across it.
The p.d. varies at the same frequency as the sound (and its size depends on the loudness).
exam.tip: Follow the chain sound, diaphragm, coil, field, induced p.d.

exam.q: State the difference between the output of an alternator and a dynamo and explain what causes it.
model: An alternator produces a.c.; a dynamo produces d.c.
An alternator uses slip rings, so each end of the coil stays connected to the same brush and the output reverses every half turn.
A dynamo uses a split-ring commutator which swaps the connections every half turn so the output is always the same direction.
exam.tip: Name the component in each case.

exam.q: Explain why the induced p.d. from a rotating coil is zero when the coil is perpendicular to the magnetic field.
model: At that instant the coil sides move parallel to the field lines.
So they do not cut field lines and no p.d. is induced.
exam.tip: Contrast with parallel position where cutting is fastest.

exam.q: A graph shows the output of an alternator. Describe how the graph changes if the coil is turned twice as fast.
model: The peak p.d. (amplitude) increases (doubles).
The frequency doubles: twice as many cycles in the same time (period halves).
exam.tip: Always mention two changes for faster rotation.

exam.q: An alternator coil turns 50 times per second. State the frequency of the a.c. produced.
model: 50 Hz
exam.tip: One rotation gives one complete cycle.

exam.q: Describe how electromagnetic induction is used in an alternator to generate alternating current.
model: A coil is rotated in a magnetic field (between the poles of a magnet).
The sides of the coil cut the magnetic field lines, so a p.d. is induced.
The p.d. is largest when the coil is parallel to the field and zero when perpendicular.
Each side moves up then down through the field, so the induced p.d. reverses every half turn.
Each end of the coil is connected to its own slip ring, with brushes connecting to the external circuit.
So the output is an alternating p.d. (one cycle per rotation); faster rotation gives a larger p.d. and higher frequency.
exam.tip: Level of response: describe the set-up, the induction, the reversal and the role of slip rings.

exam.q: Explain why it becomes harder to turn a generator when the lamp connected to it is switched on.
model: A current flows, which produces its own magnetic field that opposes the motion (change).
So more work must be done to turn the coil, and this energy is transferred to the lamp.
exam.tip: Link force opposing motion to energy transfer.

worked.q: A student moves a magnet into a coil and records a peak reading of 2 mV. Predict the reading for: (a) the magnet moved in twice as fast, (b) the magnet pulled out at the original speed, (c) a coil with three times as many turns at the original speed.
steps: (a) Moving twice as fast cuts field lines twice as fast, so the p.d. roughly doubles: about 4 mV.
(b) Pulling out reverses the change, so the p.d. reverses: about -2 mV (needle deflects the other way).
(c) Each turn adds its own p.d., so three times the turns gives about three times the p.d.: about 6 mV.
worked.ans: (a) about 4 mV, (b) about -2 mV (opposite direction), (c) about 6 mV.

worked.q: An alternator gives a peak p.d. of 6 V and a period of 0.02 s. The rotation speed is doubled. Find the new frequency and describe the new peak p.d.
steps: Original frequency f = 1 / T = 1 / 0.02 = 50 Hz.
Doubling the rotation speed doubles the number of cycles per second: new f = 100 Hz (period 0.01 s).
Turning faster means field lines are cut faster, so the peak p.d. increases; for twice the speed it is about 12 V.
worked.ans: Frequency 100 Hz; peak p.d. increases to about 12 V.

phy_ocrb.2.12.summary: A transformer is two coils of insulated wire wound on a shared soft iron core. An **alternating current** in the primary coil makes a changing magnetic field in the core, which **induces an alternating p.d.** in the secondary coil. The ratio of the p.d.s equals the **turns ratio**, Vp / Vs = Np / Ns, and for a 100% efficient transformer the power in equals the power out, so Vp × Ip = Vs × Is. This is why step-up transformers let the National Grid send electricity at a high p.d. and a small current.

core.h: What a transformer is made of
core.p: Every transformer has the same three parts. The coils are not electrically connected to each other: energy is passed from one to the other only through the **changing magnetic field** in the iron core.
bullets: **Primary coil**: the input coil, connected to the alternating supply (p.d. Vp, Np turns).
**Secondary coil**: the output coil, connected to the device or load (p.d. Vs, Ns turns).
**Soft iron core**: links the two coils so that almost all the magnetic field made by the primary passes through the secondary.
Iron is used because it is **easily magnetised and demagnetised**, so its magnetism can reverse many times a second as the current alternates.
The wire is **insulated** so the current flows round the turns rather than short-circuiting across them or into the core.

callouts.p: A device that changes the size of an alternating potential difference, made of a primary coil and a secondary coil wound on an iron core.

fig.cap: Structure of a transformer. The a.c. supply drives current in the primary coil; the changing magnetic field is carried round the soft iron core and induces a p.d. across the secondary coil, which drives current through the load.

core.p: A transformer uses **electromagnetic induction**: a p.d. is induced in a conductor when the magnetic field through it changes. The chain of reasoning is a favourite 4 to 6 mark question, so learn it in order.
bullets: 1. An **alternating current** flows in the primary coil.
2. This produces a magnetic field in the iron core that is **constantly changing** (growing, shrinking and reversing direction).
3. The iron core carries this changing magnetic field through the secondary coil.
4. The changing magnetic field **induces an alternating p.d.** across the secondary coil.
5. If the secondary is part of a complete circuit, the induced p.d. drives an **alternating current** in it.
The output is a.c. with the **same frequency** as the input.

callouts.t: The word that earns the mark
callouts.p: Always say the magnetic field is CHANGING. A steady field induces nothing.

core.h: Why transformers only work with a.c.
core.p: Induction needs a change. A direct current gives a steady magnetic field, so after the instant of switching on nothing is changing and no p.d. is induced in the secondary.
bullets: **d.c. in primary** gives a constant magnetic field, so **no p.d. is induced** in the secondary (except briefly at switch on or switch off).
**a.c. in primary** gives a continuously changing field, so a p.d. is induced all the time.
This is one reason mains electricity and the National Grid use **alternating current**.

callouts.p: A transformer does not convert a.c. into d.c. or change the frequency. It only changes the size of the alternating p.d. (and current).

core.p: The p.d. across each coil is proportional to its number of turns, because each turn of the secondary has the same changing field through it and the induced p.d.s in the turns add up. So doubling the secondary turns doubles the output p.d.
bullets: **Vp / Vs = Np / Ns** (potential difference across primary / p.d. across secondary = turns on primary / turns on secondary).
Vp and Vs in volts (V); Np and Ns are just numbers of turns (no unit).
Equivalently **Vs = Vp × Ns / Np**, useful when finding the output p.d.
The **turns ratio** is Np : Ns (or Ns / Np), a ratio with no unit.
The equation can be written either way up, as long as primary and secondary are both on top (or both on the bottom).

callouts.t: Equation (given on the equation sheet, triple)
callouts.p: potential difference across primary coil / potential difference across secondary coil = number of turns in primary coil / number of turns in secondary coil
Write the equation, substitute with units, then rearrange. Do a sanity check: more secondary turns must mean a bigger output p.d.

core.p: Which way the p.d. changes depends only on which coil has more turns.
bullets: **Step-up transformer**: Ns greater than Np, so Vs greater than Vp. The current in the secondary is smaller than in the primary.
**Step-down transformer**: Ns less than Np, so Vs less than Vp. The current in the secondary is larger than in the primary.
Step-up: used at power stations to raise the p.d. for transmission.
Step-down: used near homes (substations) to lower it to a safe 230 V, and in phone chargers and adapters to lower mains to a few volts.

core.p: A transformer cannot create energy. If it is **100% efficient**, all the electrical power supplied to the primary is delivered by the secondary. Since electrical power = p.d. × current, this gives the second transformer equation.
bullets: **Vp × Ip = Vs × Is** for a 100% efficient transformer.
Ip = current in primary (A); Is = current in secondary (A).
So if the p.d. is stepped up by a factor of 10, the current is stepped **down** by a factor of 10.
Combining the two equations: **Is / Ip = Np / Ns** (the current ratio is the inverse of the turns ratio).
A step-up transformer does **not** give you more power: it trades current for p.d.

callouts.p: potential difference across primary coil × current in primary coil = potential difference across secondary coil × current in secondary coil
Students often think a step-up transformer increases the current too. It cannot: that would mean more power out than in, breaking conservation of energy.

core.p: Real transformers are very efficient (often over 95%) but not perfect, so in practice power out is slightly less than power in. The wasted energy is dissipated as heat.
bullets: **Heating of the coils**: current in the resistance of the copper wire transfers energy by heating.
**Heating of the core**: the changing field also induces small currents in the iron core itself, which heat it. Cores are made of thin insulated sheets (**laminated**) to reduce this.
Some magnetic field may not pass through the secondary coil.
Efficiency = useful power output / total power input (× 100 for a percentage), so for a transformer efficiency = (Vs × Is) / (Vp × Ip).
Large transformers need cooling (for example oil and cooling fins) because of this heating.

callouts.p: Unless a question says otherwise, assume the transformer is 100% efficient when using Vp × Ip = Vs × Is.

core.h: Why the National Grid uses step-up transformers
core.p: The power lost as heat in the transmission cables is P = I² × R. Because power depends on the **square** of the current, cutting the current makes a huge difference. Step-up transformers raise the p.d. so the same power is sent with a much smaller current.
bullets: Same power transmitted: P = V × I, so a higher V means a lower I.
Power lost in cables = I² × R: halving the current cuts the heating loss to **one quarter**.
A 10 times higher p.d. gives 1/10 of the current and **1/100** of the power loss.
Smaller current also means thinner, lighter, cheaper cables and pylons can be used.
Step-down transformers then reduce the p.d. in stages to 230 V because very high p.d.s are dangerous in homes.
UK figures: power stations generate at roughly 25 kV; transmission cables are at up to 400 kV; homes receive 230 V.

callouts.p: High p.d. means low current, which means less energy dissipated as heat in the cables, so transmission is more efficient.

core.h: Using the turns ratio equation step by step
core.p: Most marks come from calculations, so use a fixed routine every time.
bullets: Write down the known values with units: Vp, Vs, Np, Ns, Ip, Is.
Choose the equation: turns are mentioned, so use Vp / Vs = Np / Ns; currents are mentioned, so use Vp × Ip = Vs × Is.
Rearrange before substituting if you can, for example Ns = Np × Vs / Vp.
Convert kV to V (1 kV = 1000 V) and mA to A if needed.
Check: a bigger p.d. must go with more turns and a smaller current.
Turns must be a whole number; p.d. and current answers usually go to 2 or 3 significant figures.

core.p: Transformers are everywhere that mains electricity has to be matched to a device.
bullets: Phone and laptop chargers: step-down transformers reduce 230 V to a few volts (then a circuit converts it to d.c.).
Substations: step down from grid p.d.s to local distribution p.d.s and then to 230 V.
Power stations: step up to hundreds of kilovolts.
Low voltage lighting and model railways use step-down transformers.
Isolating transformers (1 : 1) keep a device electrically separate from the mains for safety, as there is no wire connection between the coils.

core.p: Top answers connect the transformer to other parts of P3 and show why each step happens.
bullets: The primary coil is basically an electromagnet with a reversing current (link to P3.5 solenoids).
The secondary works like a generator with no moving parts: the field changes instead of a magnet moving (link to P3.7 induction).
The output frequency equals the input frequency because the field reverses at the same rate as the primary current.
If the secondary circuit is open, there is still an induced p.d. but no secondary current, so almost no power is drawn.
More secondary turns means more turns cutting the same changing field, so more induced p.d. in total.

callouts.p: Structure: parts of a transformer, then a.c. causes a changing field, then induced p.d., then turns ratio and power equation, then application to the grid with I² R.

analogy.p: A transformer is like a bicycle gear system. Changing gear changes how fast your wheel spins compared with your pedals, but it cannot give you more energy than your legs put in: if the wheel turns faster, it pushes with less force. In the same way a transformer can raise the p.d. (like speed) but only by lowering the current (like force), so the power stays the same. The turns ratio is like the gear ratio. Where it breaks down: gears work with steady motion, but a transformer only works when the current keeps changing (a.c.), and a transformer passes energy through a magnetic field, with no physical link between the coils.

terms.d: A device with primary and secondary coils on an iron core that changes the size of an alternating p.d.
The input coil of a transformer, connected to the alternating supply.
The output coil of a transformer, in which a p.d. is induced.
Soft iron that links the coils and carries the changing magnetic field from primary to secondary; easily magnetised and demagnetised.
The ratio of the number of turns on the primary coil to the number on the secondary coil, Np : Ns.
A transformer with more turns on the secondary than the primary, so the output p.d. is greater than the input p.d.
A transformer with fewer turns on the secondary than the primary, so the output p.d. is less than the input p.d.
The production of a potential difference across a conductor when the magnetic field through it changes.
A potential difference produced in a conductor by a changing magnetic field.
Current that repeatedly reverses direction.
Current that flows in one direction only.
The energy transferred per unit charge between two points, measured in volts.
Useful power output divided by total power input.
The network of cables and transformers that links power stations to consumers across the country.
An iron core made of thin insulated sheets to reduce heating caused by currents induced in the core.

mistakes.w: Transformers work with d.c.
mistakes.r: A transformer needs a.c., because only a changing magnetic field induces a p.d. in the secondary.

mistakes.w: Current flows from the primary coil to the secondary coil through the core.
mistakes.r: The coils are insulated from each other; the changing magnetic field in the core induces a p.d. in the secondary.

mistakes.w: A magnetic field is induced in the secondary.
mistakes.r: A potential difference (voltage) is induced in the secondary coil by the changing magnetic field.

mistakes.w: A step-up transformer increases the power.
mistakes.r: Power out is at most equal to power in: Vp × Ip = Vs × Is. Higher p.d. means smaller current.

mistakes.w: Step-up transformers increase the current to reduce losses.
mistakes.r: They increase the p.d. and so decrease the current; smaller current means less I² R heating in the cables.

mistakes.w: Writing Vp / Vs = Ns / Np.
mistakes.r: Primary goes with primary: Vp / Vs = Np / Ns.

mistakes.w: The core is made of steel or copper.
mistakes.r: Soft iron, because it is easily magnetised and demagnetised as the field reverses.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to convert kV to V in Vp × Ip = Vs × Is.
mistakes.r: Use consistent units: 1 kV = 1000 V, 1 mA = 0.001 A.

mistakes.w: High voltage makes electricity travel faster.
mistakes.r: High p.d. means a lower current for the same power, so less energy is dissipated as heat in the cables.

exam.q: State what is meant by a step-down transformer.
model: A transformer whose output (secondary) p.d. is less than its input (primary) p.d. / which has fewer turns on the secondary coil than the primary.
exam.tip: Either the p.d. or the turns description earns the mark.

exam.q: Explain why a transformer will not work with a direct current supply.
model: d.c. produces a constant / unchanging magnetic field in the core.
So no p.d. is induced in the secondary coil (induction needs a changing field).
exam.tip: Use the word changing or unchanging.

exam.q: Explain why the core of a transformer is made from iron.
model: Iron is easily magnetised (and demagnetised) / is a magnetic material.
So it links the magnetic field from the primary to the secondary coil / increases the field through the secondary.
exam.tip: Say what iron does, then why that helps.

exam.q: A transformer has 200 turns on its primary coil and 4000 turns on its secondary coil. The input p.d. is 12 V. Calculate the output p.d.
model: Vs = 240 V
exam.tip: More turns on the secondary, so the answer must be bigger than 12 V.

exam.q: A phone charger steps 230 V down to 5.0 V. The secondary coil has 50 turns. Calculate the number of turns on the primary coil.
model: Vp / Vs = Np / Ns
Np = 2300 turns
exam.tip: Step-down, so the primary must have more turns.

exam.q: A 100% efficient transformer has an input of 230 V and 0.50 A. Its output p.d. is 11.5 V. Calculate the output current.
model: Vp × Ip = Vs × Is
Is = 10 A
exam.tip: p.d. stepped down by 20 times, so current stepped up by 20 times.

exam.q: A step-up transformer at a power station changes 25 kV to 400 kV. The current in the primary coil is 3200 A. Calculate the current in the transmission cables, assuming the transformer is 100% efficient.
model: Vp × Ip = Vs × Is
Is = 200 A
exam.tip: Kilovolts cancel if both are in kV, but converting is safest.

exam.q: Describe how a transformer produces an output p.d. across the secondary coil.
model: Alternating current in the primary coil.
Produces a changing magnetic field (in the core).
Iron core links / carries the changing field to the secondary coil.
Changing field induces an (alternating) p.d. across the secondary coil.
exam.tip: Four steps, four marks: keep them in order.

exam.q: The output power of a real transformer is less than its input power. Explain why, and suggest one way it is reduced.
model: Energy is dissipated as heat in the coils (resistance of wire) / in the core.
Use low resistance (thick copper) wire / a laminated core.
exam.tip: Name where the heating happens.

exam.q: Explain why electricity is transmitted across the National Grid at a very high potential difference, and why it is then reduced before reaching homes. Use ideas about transformers and power in your answer.
model: Step-up transformer increases the p.d. (secondary has more turns than primary).
For the same power, P = V × I, so the current is reduced (Vp × Ip = Vs × Is).
Power lost in cables = I² × R, so lower current means much less energy dissipated as heat.
Halving current reduces losses to a quarter; transmission is more efficient.
Thinner / cheaper cables can be used.
Step-down transformers reduce the p.d. to 230 V because high p.d. is dangerous in homes.
exam.tip: Level 3 answers link all three ideas: transformer action, P = VI trade-off and I² R heating.

worked.q: A transformer has 500 turns on the primary coil. It is connected to a 230 V a.c. supply and must give an output of 46 V. How many turns are needed on the secondary coil? Is it step-up or step-down?
steps: Write the equation: Vp / Vs = Np / Ns.
Rearrange for Ns: Ns = Np × Vs / Vp.
Substitute: Ns = 500 × 46 / 230.
Calculate: Ns = 500 × 0.2 = 100 turns.
Ns is less than Np, so it is a step-down transformer.
worked.ans: 100 turns; step-down transformer.

worked.q: A 100% efficient step-up transformer increases the p.d. from 20 kV to 200 kV. The input current is 500 A. (a) Find the output current. (b) The cables have a total resistance of 4.0 ohms. Compare the power lost in the cables with and without the transformer.
steps: (a) Vp × Ip = Vs × Is, so Is = Vp × Ip / Vs.
(b) Without the transformer the current would be 500 A: P = I² × R = 500² × 4.0 = 1 000 000 W = 1.0 MW.
With the transformer: P = 50² × 4.0 = 10 000 W = 10 kW.
Ratio: 1 000 000 / 10 000 = 100, so the loss is 100 times smaller.
This matches the rule: p.d. up 10 times, current down 10 times, loss down 10² = 100 times.
worked.ans: (a) 50 A. (b) 1.0 MW lost without the transformer, 10 kW with it: one hundredth of the loss.

worked.q: A step-down transformer has a turns ratio Np : Ns of 40 : 1. The secondary supplies 6.0 V and 2.0 A to a lamp. Find the primary p.d. and the primary current (assume 100% efficiency).
steps: Vp / Vs = Np / Ns = 40, so Vp = 40 × 6.0 = 240 V.
Power out = Vs × Is = 6.0 × 2.0 = 12 W.
Power in = power out, so Vp × Ip = 12 W.
Check: current ratio Is / Ip = 2.0 / 0.050 = 40, the inverse of the p.d. ratio.

phy_ocrb.2.4.summary: **Potential difference (p.d.)** is the energy transferred (work done) per unit charge as charge moves between two points: 1 volt = 1 joule per coulomb. In a **series circuit** the current is the same everywhere and the p.d.s across the components add up to the supply p.d.; in a **parallel circuit** every branch has the same p.d. as the supply and the branch currents add up to the total current. Both rules come from two conservation laws: **charge is conserved** (current rules) and **energy is conserved** (p.d. rules), and you test them in PAG7 by building circuits and measuring with ammeters and voltmeters.

core.p: A battery or power supply does work on the charges in a circuit, giving them energy. As the charges pass through components such as lamps and resistors they do work, transferring that energy to the surroundings. **Potential difference** measures how much energy is transferred for every coulomb of charge that moves between two points.
bullets: **p.d. = work done (energy transferred) ÷ charge**, written V = W ÷ Q
Units: potential difference in **volts (V)**, energy in **joules (J)**, charge in **coulombs (C)**
**1 volt = 1 joule per coulomb** (1 V = 1 J/C)
A 6 V battery gives each coulomb of charge 6 J of energy as it passes through
Across a component, a p.d. of 2 V means each coulomb transfers 2 J of energy to that component
P.d. is always measured **between two points**, never 'at' a point or 'through' a component
Older word: voltage. Mark schemes accept 'p.d.' and prefer it

callouts.p: The potential difference between two points is the work done (energy transferred) per unit charge passing between those points.
1 volt is a potential difference of 1 joule per coulomb.

core.p: The same relationship can be used three ways. Always convert to base units first: charge in coulombs, energy in joules. The P3.4 equation 'energy transferred = charge × p.d.' is just this definition rearranged.
bullets: V = W ÷ Q (find the p.d.)
W = Q × V (find the energy transferred)
Q = W ÷ V (find the charge)
If you know current and time, find charge first with Q = I × t
kJ to J: multiply by 1000; mC to C: divide by 1000
Large p.d. with small charge can transfer the same energy as small p.d. with large charge

callouts.p: Learn V = W ÷ Q by heart. Write the equation, substitute with units, then give the answer with its unit: each is often a separate mark.

core.p: A voltmeter compares the energy per coulomb at two points, so it must be connected **across** the component, with one lead on each side. This is called connecting it **in parallel**. An ideal voltmeter has a very high resistance so almost no current flows through it and it does not change the circuit it is measuring.
bullets: Voltmeter: connected **in parallel** across the component
Ammeter: connected **in series** so all the current flows through it
Voltmeter has a **very high resistance** (ideally infinite)
Ammeter has a **very low resistance** (ideally zero)
Connecting a voltmeter in series would almost stop the current because of its huge resistance
Connecting an ammeter in parallel would short circuit the component and could damage the meter
Digital meters: check the range and zero reading before use

callouts.p: Students often say a voltmeter measures the 'voltage through' a lamp. P.d. is across a component; current is through it.

fig.cap: An ammeter is connected in series on the wire, so the same current passes through it. A voltmeter is connected in parallel across the resistor, one lead on each side. At a junction, the current going in (3.0 A) equals the total current coming out (2.0 A + 1.0 A) because charge is conserved.

core.p: In a series circuit there is only **one path** for the charge. Charge cannot be created, destroyed or stored in a wire, so every coulomb that leaves the cell must pass through every component and return. That means the rate of flow of charge, the current, is the **same at every point** in the loop.
bullets: Same current everywhere: I = I1 = I2 = I3
An ammeter reads the same wherever it is placed in a series loop
Current is **not used up** by components: the charge comes back to the cell
What is 'used up' is energy, not charge or current
If one component breaks (open circuit), the current stops everywhere
Adding more components in series increases total resistance, so the current is smaller

callouts.p: Current is the same at all points in a series circuit because charge is conserved.

core.p: The supply gives each coulomb a fixed amount of energy. As that coulomb travels round a series loop it passes through each component in turn and gives away some of that energy in each one. By the time it returns to the cell it has given away all of it. So the p.d.s across the components **add up to the supply p.d.**
bullets: V(supply) = V1 + V2 + V3 + ...
This is **conservation of energy**: energy given per coulomb = energy transferred per coulomb
The p.d. **shares** between components in series
The component with the **larger resistance** gets the **larger share** of the p.d. (since V = IR and I is the same)
Two identical lamps in series on 6 V each get 3 V, so each is dimmer than one lamp alone on 6 V
Ratio rule: V1 ÷ V2 = R1 ÷ R2 in series

callouts.t: Why the bigger resistor gets more p.d.
callouts.p: Same current flows through both, and V = I × R, so the bigger R needs a bigger V to push the same current through.

core.h: Following one coulomb round a series circuit
core.p: A good grade 9 explanation tracks the energy of one coulomb of charge. It gains energy in the cell, then loses energy in steps across each resistor, and has none of the cell's energy left when it gets back. The wires are treated as having negligible resistance, so almost no energy is transferred in them and the potential stays almost the same along a wire.
bullets: In the cell: each coulomb gains 6 J (6 V)
Across R1: each coulomb transfers 2 J (2 V)
Across R2: each coulomb transfers 4 J (4 V)
Total transferred 2 J + 4 J = 6 J = energy gained
P.d. across a plain connecting wire is about 0 V
Energy is transferred in components by heating (resistor) or by heating and light (lamp)

fig.cap: Energy per coulomb (potential) as you go round the series circuit. The cell raises the potential by 6 V, so each coulomb gains 6 J. The potential stays level along the wires, then drops by 2 V across R1 and by 4 V across R2, returning to 0. The gains equal the losses, which is conservation of energy.

core.p: In a parallel circuit each branch connects **directly across the supply**. A coulomb can only go through one branch, and whichever branch it takes it must give away all the energy it gained in the cell before it gets back. So the p.d. across every branch is the **same as the supply p.d.**
bullets: V(supply) = V1 = V2 = V3
Each branch behaves as if it were connected to the supply on its own
Two identical lamps in parallel on a 3 V cell each get the full 3 V, so each is as bright as one lamp alone
That is why houses wire lights and sockets in parallel: every device gets the full mains p.d.
Each branch can be switched on and off independently
If one branch breaks, the others keep working

callouts.p: Components connected in parallel all have the same potential difference across them.

core.p: At a **junction** the current splits between the branches and then recombines. Because charge is conserved, the total current flowing into a junction equals the total current flowing out. So the branch currents add up to the current in the main part of the circuit.
bullets: I(total) = I1 + I2 + I3
The branch with the **smaller resistance** takes the **larger current** (I = V ÷ R with the same V)
Identical branches share the current equally
Adding another branch gives the charge an extra path, so the **total current increases**
The current in the existing branches stays the same (same p.d., same resistance)
So the cell has to supply more current and runs down faster

callouts.p: The sum of the currents flowing into a junction equals the sum of the currents flowing out, because charge is conserved.

core.h: Series versus parallel at a glance
core.p: Most exam questions on this point ask you to apply one of four rules. Learn them in a grid, and always be ready to say which conservation law each one comes from.
bullets: Current rules come from **conservation of charge**
P.d. rules come from **conservation of energy**
Series: current same, p.d. shared
Parallel: p.d. same, current shared

head: Series
Parallel
rows: Splits; branch currents add to total
Same across each branch as supply
Several paths, each across the supply

callouts.p: In 'explain' questions, a top answer says 'because charge is conserved' or 'because energy is conserved' rather than only stating the rule.

core.h: Cells and batteries in series and parallel
core.p: A battery is two or more cells joined together. When cells are connected in series facing the same way, each coulomb passes through every cell and gains energy in each, so their p.d.s add. If one cell is reversed it takes energy back off the charge and cancels out another cell.
bullets: Cells in series, same direction: total p.d. = sum, e.g. 3 × 1.5 V = 4.5 V
One cell reversed: subtract its p.d., e.g. 1.5 + 1.5 - 1.5 = 1.5 V
Identical cells in parallel: total p.d. is the same as one cell, but they last longer
Long line on the cell symbol is the **positive terminal**
Conventional current flows out of the positive terminal round the circuit to the negative terminal
Electrons actually flow the other way, from negative to positive

core.p: Exam circuits often mix series and parallel parts. Work them one rule at a time: treat the parallel block as one unit in series with the rest, then use the parallel rules inside the block.
bullets: The p.d. across a parallel block is the same for every branch in that block
The p.d. across the block plus the p.d. across the series parts = supply p.d.
The current through the series part equals the total current entering the parallel block
Use V = IR on each component separately with that component's own V and I
Always label each answer with which component it belongs to

callouts.p: When using V = IR on one component, use the p.d. across that component only, not the supply p.d.

core.h: PAG7: investigating series and parallel circuits
core.p: In this practical activity you build series and parallel circuits from a low-voltage supply, lamps or resistors, an ammeter and a voltmeter, and test the rules by measurement. It also develops skills in drawing circuit diagrams and connecting meters correctly.
bullets: Draw the circuit diagram first, using standard symbols
Series: measure current at several points (between each component); readings should be equal
Series: measure p.d. across each component and across the supply; component p.d.s should add to the supply p.d.
Parallel: measure current in the main circuit and in each branch; branch currents should add to the total
Parallel: measure p.d. across each branch; all should equal the supply p.d.
Use the same meter for comparisons to reduce systematic error from meter calibration
Switch off between readings so components do not heat up and change resistance
Repeat readings and calculate a mean; small differences come from meter resolution and resistance of wires and connections
Safety: low p.d. supply; lamps and resistors can get hot

head: Variable type
Example
rows: Supply p.d., same components, same meters

callouts.p: If p.d.s add to slightly less than the supply, explain it by the small resistance of the connecting wires and contacts, or meter resolution, not by 'energy being lost'.

analogy.p: Picture skiers (charges) on a mountain. The ski lift (the cell) does work lifting each skier to the top, giving them gravitational energy (p.d. is like height per skier). Coming down, a skier on a single run (series) passes several steep sections (resistors) one after another, losing a bit of height on each; the drops add up to the total height of the lift. If the run splits into several separate slopes (parallel branches), each skier takes only one slope, but every slope falls the full height of the mountain, so each branch has the full p.d. The number of skiers passing a point per minute is the current: skiers are never lost, so the flow into a fork equals the total flow out. Where it breaks down: real skiers move independently and can stop, while charges in a circuit all start moving almost at once throughout the wire and do not pile up anywhere; also the lift carries skiers one way, whereas p.d. is a property between two points, not a height of one charge.

terms.d: Work done (energy transferred) per unit charge between two points in a circuit; measured in volts.
Unit of potential difference; 1 V = 1 joule per coulomb.
Energy transferred when a force moves something, here when charge is pushed through a component; measured in joules.
Property of particles such as electrons; the amount flowing is measured in coulombs (C).
Unit of charge; the charge passing a point when a current of 1 A flows for 1 s.
Rate of flow of charge; measured in amperes (A).
Meter that measures p.d.; connected in parallel across a component; very high resistance.
Meter that measures current; connected in series; very low resistance.
Circuit with only one path for the charge; components connected end to end in one loop.
Circuit with two or more branches, each connected across the supply, giving charge more than one path.
Point where a circuit splits into branches or branches join; current in equals current out.
Charge cannot be created or destroyed; explains the current rules in series and parallel circuits.
Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred; explains why p.d.s round a loop add up to the supply p.d.
One of the separate paths in a parallel circuit.
The potential difference provided by the cell, battery or power supply; energy given to each coulomb.
Current direction shown from the positive terminal round the circuit to the negative terminal; opposite to electron flow.

mistakes.w: Current gets used up by each lamp, so it is smaller after the lamp.
mistakes.r: Current is the same everywhere in a series circuit; charge is conserved. It is energy that is transferred in each component.

mistakes.w: The voltage through the resistor is 3 V.
mistakes.r: The potential difference across the resistor is 3 V; current flows through, p.d. is across.

mistakes.w: Voltmeter is connected in series.
mistakes.r: Voltmeter is connected in parallel (across the component); the ammeter goes in series.

mistakes.w: In parallel the p.d. is shared between the branches.
mistakes.r: Each parallel branch has the same p.d. as the supply; it is the current that is shared.

mistakes.w: P.d. is the energy of the charge.
mistakes.r: P.d. is energy transferred per unit charge (per coulomb) between two points.

mistakes.w: Adding a lamp in parallel makes all the lamps dimmer.
mistakes.r: Each lamp still has the full supply p.d., so brightness is unchanged; the total current from the supply increases.

mistakes.w: In series both resistors get the same p.d.
mistakes.r: Only if they are identical; the larger resistance has the larger p.d. because the current is the same and V = IR.

mistakes.w: 1 volt is 1 joule per second.
mistakes.r: 1 volt is 1 joule per coulomb; 1 joule per second is 1 watt.

mistakes.w: The p.d.s add up because voltage is conserved.
mistakes.r: The p.d.s add up to the supply p.d. because energy is conserved.

exam.q: State what is meant by a potential difference of 1 volt.
model: 1 joule of energy transferred per coulomb of charge (1 J/C)
exam.tip: Say 'per coulomb', not 'per second'.

exam.q: Describe how a voltmeter should be connected to measure the p.d. across a lamp.
model: In parallel with / across the lamp (one lead each side)
exam.tip: The word 'parallel' or 'across' is the mark.

exam.q: A battery transfers 360 J of energy to 60 C of charge. Calculate the p.d. of the battery.
exam.tip: Write the equation first; the unit is part of the final mark.

exam.q: Two resistors are in series with a 9.0 V battery. The p.d. across one resistor is 3.5 V. Calculate the p.d. across the other resistor and explain your answer.
model: p.d.s in series add up to the supply p.d. / energy is conserved
exam.tip: Explain questions need the reason, not just the number.

exam.q: In a parallel circuit the main current is 1.2 A. One branch carries 0.45 A. Calculate the current in the other branch.
exam.tip: Branch currents add to the total.

exam.q: Explain why the current is the same at every point in a series circuit.
model: There is only one path for the charge
Charge is conserved / not used up, so the same charge passes every point per second
exam.tip: Use 'charge is conserved', not 'current is conserved'.

exam.q: Two identical lamps are connected first in series and then in parallel to the same 6 V battery. Compare the brightness of the lamps in each circuit and explain.
model: In series each lamp has 3 V across it / p.d. is shared
In parallel each lamp has the full 6 V
So the parallel lamps have a bigger current / more energy per coulomb / more power
Parallel lamps are brighter
exam.tip: Link p.d. to current and energy transfer, then to brightness.

exam.q: Calculate the energy transferred when 0.25 A flows through a 12 V lamp for 2 minutes.
exam.tip: Convert minutes to seconds before anything else.

exam.q: A student builds a parallel circuit with three branches. She adds a fourth identical branch. Describe and explain what happens to the current from the supply.
model: Total current from the supply increases
The new branch has the full supply p.d. so it draws its own current
The current in the other branches stays the same, and branch currents add to the total
exam.tip: State the change, then give two linked reasons.

exam.q: Describe how you would use a battery, two lamps, an ammeter, a voltmeter and connecting wires to show that the current rule and the p.d. rule are true for a series circuit and for a parallel circuit.
model: Draw/build a series circuit of battery and two lamps
Place the ammeter at different points in the series loop; readings should be equal
Connect the voltmeter across each lamp in turn and across the battery; lamp p.d.s should add to battery p.d.
Build a parallel circuit with each lamp on its own branch
Ammeter in main circuit and in each branch; branch currents should add to main current
Voltmeter across each branch shows the same p.d. as the battery; repeat readings and compare; explain small differences by meter resolution / wire resistance
exam.tip: A level 3 answer covers both circuits, both meters connected correctly, and what the results should show.

worked.q: A 12 V battery is connected to a lamp. In 5 minutes, 450 C of charge flows through the lamp. Calculate the energy transferred by the lamp.
steps: Write the equation: W = Q × V
The lamp is the only component, so the p.d. across it = 12 V
Substitute: W = 450 × 12

worked.q: A 6.0 V battery is connected to resistors R1 (4 ohms) and R2 (8 ohms) in series. The current is 0.50 A. Find the p.d. across each resistor and check the p.d. rule.
steps: Current is the same through both: I = 0.50 A
Check: 2.0 + 4.0 = 6.0 V = supply p.d., as energy conservation predicts
The larger resistor (8 ohms) has twice the p.d. of the smaller one
worked.ans: 2.0 V across R1 and 4.0 V across R2, which add to 6.0 V

worked.q: A 3.0 V cell is connected to two lamps in parallel. Lamp A has resistance 5 ohms and lamp B has resistance 10 ohms. Find the current in each lamp and the total current from the cell.
steps: In parallel, each lamp has the full 3.0 V across it
Total current = 0.60 + 0.30 = 0.90 A (junction rule, charge conserved)
worked.ans: 0.60 A in A, 0.30 A in B, 0.90 A total

phy_ocrb.2.5.summary: Adding resistors **in series** increases the total resistance (R = R1 + R2) because the charge has to pass through every resistor, while adding resistors **in parallel** decreases the total resistance, to less than the smallest branch, because the charge gets extra paths. **Light-dependent resistors (LDRs)** have a resistance that falls as light intensity rises, and **thermistors** have a resistance that falls as temperature rises. Placed in series with a fixed resistor as a **potential divider**, they make **sensing circuits** whose output p.d. changes with light or temperature, used to switch on street lights, heaters and fire alarms.

core.p: Resistance tells you how hard it is for current to flow through a component. For a given p.d., a bigger resistance means a smaller current. This point is about what happens to the **total (net) resistance** when you combine resistors, and how resistors that change their resistance can be used to sense the world.
bullets: R = V ÷ I, so V = I × R
Resistance measured in **ohms (Ω)**
Total resistance of a circuit decides the current drawn from the supply: I = V(supply) ÷ R(total)
Use the total resistance only with the supply p.d.; use each resistor's own p.d. for that resistor

callouts.p: Resistance = potential difference ÷ current; it is measured in ohms.

core.p: In series, the same current flows through every resistor, and the p.d.s add up. Each resistor needs its own share of p.d. to push the current through, so the total p.d. needed for each amp of current is the sum of all of them. That is why **series resistances simply add**.
bullets: Total resistance is **bigger than any single resistor**
Adding another resistor in series always increases total resistance and decreases current
Reason: charge must pass through **every** resistor, one after another; there is only one path
Proof: V = V1 + V2 = IR1 + IR2 = I(R1 + R2)
Example: 2 Ω + 4 Ω = 6 Ω

callouts.p: The total resistance of resistors in series is the sum of their resistances.

fig.cap: Left: 2 Ω and 4 Ω in series give a total of 6 Ω, more than either one alone. Right: two 6 Ω resistors in parallel give a total of 3 Ω, less than the smallest branch, because the charge has two paths to choose from.

core.p: In parallel, each resistor is connected directly across the supply and has the full p.d. Each branch therefore draws its own current, and the branch currents add. Adding another branch means **more total current for the same p.d.**, and since R = V ÷ I, a bigger total current means a **smaller total resistance**.
bullets: Adding resistors in parallel **decreases** the total resistance
Total resistance is **less than the smallest** individual resistance
Reason: extra branch = **extra path** for the charge, so more charge flows per second
Same p.d. across each branch, so each branch current I = V ÷ R(branch)
Two **identical** resistors in parallel: total = half of one, e.g. 6 Ω and 6 Ω gives 3 Ω
Find total resistance by working out total current and using R = V(supply) ÷ I(total)

callouts.p: 6 Ω in parallel with 6 Ω is NOT 12 Ω. Adding R values only works in series.
For 'explain why total resistance decreases', say: same p.d. across each branch, extra branch carries extra current, so total current increases, so R = V ÷ I is smaller.

core.p: A quick comparison helps you predict answers without calculating, for example whether a total resistance should be bigger or smaller than one you are given.
bullets: Series: more resistors means more resistance, less current
Parallel: more branches means less resistance, more current
Check answers: series total above biggest, parallel total below smallest

core.p: An LDR is made of a semiconductor. When more light falls on it, more charge carriers are freed in the material, so it conducts better. Its resistance is very high in the dark and falls steeply as light intensity increases.
bullets: **Light intensity increases, resistance decreases**
Dark: resistance high (can be many kΩ or MΩ); bright: low (a few hundred Ω)
Graph of resistance against light intensity: a curve falling steeply then levelling off
Symbol: a resistor box inside a circle with two arrows pointing **in** (light going in)
Uses: automatic street lights, night lights, security lights, camera light meters
On an I–V graph at constant light it behaves like an ohmic resistor; brighter gives a steeper line

callouts.p: The resistance of an LDR decreases as light intensity increases.

fig.cap: How an LDR and a thermistor respond. The LDR's resistance falls as light intensity increases. The thermistor's resistance falls as temperature increases. Both curves fall steeply at first and then level off.

core.p: A thermistor is also a semiconductor device. Heating it frees more charge carriers, so it conducts better. The usual GCSE thermistor is an **NTC** (negative temperature coefficient) type: its resistance falls as temperature rises.
bullets: **Temperature increases, resistance decreases**
Cold: high resistance; hot: low resistance
Graph of resistance against temperature: curve falling and levelling off
Symbol: resistor box with a diagonal line through it that has a short flat 'foot' at one end
Uses: thermostats in heating systems, fire alarms, fridges and freezers, car engine temperature sensors, digital thermometers
Opposite trend to a metal wire or filament lamp, whose resistance increases when hot

callouts.p: The resistance of a thermistor decreases as temperature increases.

callouts.t: Do not mix up the lamp
callouts.p: A filament lamp's resistance goes UP as it gets hotter. A thermistor's goes DOWN.

core.h: Sensing circuits: the potential divider idea
core.p: A sensing circuit puts a sensor (LDR or thermistor) **in series** with a fixed resistor across a supply. Because they are in series, the supply p.d. is **shared** between them in the ratio of their resistances. When the sensor's resistance changes, the share of p.d. across each component changes. The p.d. across one of them is used as the **output p.d.** to trigger something else, such as a switch, buzzer or lamp.
bullets: Same current through both components (series)
V(sensor) + V(fixed) = V(supply)
**Bigger resistance gets bigger share of p.d.**: V1 ÷ V2 = R1 ÷ R2
If the sensor's resistance **falls**, the p.d. across the sensor falls and the p.d. across the fixed resistor rises
If the sensor's resistance **rises**, the p.d. across the sensor rises and the p.d. across the fixed resistor falls
Output can be taken across either component, depending on whether you want the output to rise or fall with the condition
Output p.d. across a component = V(supply) × R(component) ÷ (R1 + R2)

callouts.p: Write the chain: condition changes, sensor resistance changes, share of p.d. changes, output p.d. changes, device switches. Each link is usually a mark.

core.h: Temperature sensing circuit (e.g. fire alarm or heater)
core.p: With the thermistor at the top and the fixed resistor at the bottom, the output is taken across the fixed resistor. When the temperature rises, the thermistor's resistance falls, so it takes a smaller share of the supply p.d., and the p.d. across the fixed resistor (the output) rises. That rising output can switch on a buzzer in a fire alarm.
bullets: Hotter: thermistor R falls, V across thermistor falls, Vout across fixed R rises: **fire alarm / cooling fan**
Swap the components (fixed resistor on top, thermistor at bottom): Vout is across the thermistor and **rises when it gets colder**: **heater / frost warning**
The output p.d. usually feeds a transistor or relay that switches a larger current
Total p.d. always stays at the supply value; only the sharing changes

fig.cap: Temperature sensing circuit (potential divider). The thermistor and fixed resistor are in series across 6 V. The output Vout is the p.d. across the fixed resistor. When it gets hotter the thermistor's resistance falls, it takes less of the 6 V, so Vout rises and can trigger an alarm.

core.h: Light sensing circuit (e.g. automatic night light)
core.p: To turn on a lamp when it gets dark, put the LDR at the bottom with the output taken across it. In the dark the LDR's resistance becomes very high, so it takes most of the supply p.d., and the output rises high enough to switch the lamp on.
bullets: Darker: LDR R rises, V across LDR rises: **street light / night light** turns on
Brighter: LDR R falls, V across LDR falls: light switches off
Swap positions so Vout is across the fixed resistor: output rises when it gets **brighter** (e.g. turning off a display, a burglar alarm triggered by light)
Same circuit idea works for any sensor whose resistance changes

callouts.p: In a potential divider, the component with the larger resistance has the larger p.d. across it.

fig.cap: Light sensing circuit for a night light. The fixed resistor and LDR are in series across 6 V and the output Vout is taken across the LDR. When it gets darker the LDR's resistance rises, it takes a bigger share of the 6 V, and Vout rises, switching on the lamp.
