core.p: Replacing the fixed resistor with a **variable resistor** lets the user set the light level or temperature at which the circuit switches. Changing the fixed resistance changes how the p.d. is shared for any given sensor resistance.
bullets: Variable resistor in place of the fixed resistor sets the **switching point (threshold)**
Example: a thermostat dial changes the temperature at which the heating turns on
The sensor's change is biggest where its graph is steepest, so the circuit is most sensitive there
A larger supply p.d. gives larger output p.d.s for the same ratio

core.h: Measurement and testing with sensing circuits
core.p: Series circuits like these are used for measuring and testing as well as switching. With a voltmeter across the fixed resistor, the reading changes with temperature or light, so after calibration the circuit can act as a thermometer or light meter. You can also investigate a sensor in the lab by measuring its resistance as conditions change.
bullets: Thermistor in a beaker of water with a thermometer; heat the water and record resistance (ohmmeter, or V and I) at regular temperatures
LDR at different distances from a lamp, or with a light meter, in a darkened room; record resistance
Stir the water and wait before each reading so the thermistor is at the water temperature
Plot resistance against temperature or light intensity and draw a smooth curve
Calibration: record output p.d. at known temperatures, then use the graph to read off unknown temperatures

callouts.p: For the thermistor keep the supply p.d. and the same thermistor; for the LDR keep the lamp power and background light the same.

core.p: Higher-level questions give resistances and ask for the output p.d. or the current. Use the series rule to find total resistance, then current, then each p.d.
bullets: Step 1: R(total) = R(sensor) + R(fixed)
Step 2: I = V(supply) ÷ R(total)
Step 3: V(component) = I × R(component)
Shortcut: V(component) = V(supply) × R(component) ÷ R(total)
Check: the two p.d.s add up to the supply p.d.

callouts.p: Convert kΩ to Ω (or keep both in kΩ) before calculating; mixing them gives answers 1000 times out.

analogy.p: Think of charges as people leaving a stadium. Resistors in series are like several narrow doorways one after another along a single corridor: every person must squeeze through every door, so each extra door slows the flow even more (resistance adds). Resistors in parallel are like extra exits side by side: each new exit lets more people out per second, so the overall 'resistance' to leaving goes down, even if the new exit is narrow. An LDR is a door that opens wider when the lights come on; a thermistor is a door that opens wider as it gets warmer. A potential divider is two doors in a corridor sharing the push from the crowd: the tighter door gets most of the push. Where it breaks down: people can bunch up and queue, but charge does not pile up in a circuit; the current is the same at every point of a series path at once.

terms.d: Potential difference across a component divided by the current through it; measured in ohms (Ω).
The single resistance that would draw the same current from the supply as the whole combination.
Resistors joined end to end so the same current passes through each; R(total) = R1 + R2 + ...
Resistors on separate branches across the same two points; total resistance is less than the smallest one.
Semiconductor resistor whose resistance decreases as light intensity increases.
Semiconductor resistor whose resistance decreases as temperature increases (NTC type).
How much light energy falls on a surface per second per unit area; brighter means higher intensity.
Component whose property (here resistance) changes in response to a change in the surroundings.
Circuit that uses a sensor so that an output changes when a condition such as light or temperature changes.
Two resistors (or a resistor and a sensor) in series across a supply, sharing the supply p.d. in the ratio of their resistances.
The p.d. across one component of a potential divider, used to control another device.
Resistor whose resistance stays constant (at constant temperature).
Resistor whose resistance can be changed; used to set the switching point of a sensing circuit.
The light level or temperature at which a sensing circuit switches a device on or off.
Material, such as silicon, whose ability to conduct changes a lot with conditions like light and temperature.
Matching readings of an instrument to known values so it can be used to measure.

mistakes.w: Two 6 Ω resistors in parallel have a total resistance of 12 Ω.
mistakes.r: In parallel the total is less than the smallest; two identical 6 Ω resistors give 3 Ω.

mistakes.w: Adding a resistor in parallel increases the resistance because there are more resistors.
mistakes.r: It decreases total resistance: an extra path means more current for the same p.d.

mistakes.w: An LDR's resistance increases in bright light.
mistakes.r: LDR resistance decreases as light intensity increases.

mistakes.w: A thermistor's resistance increases as it gets hotter, like a lamp.
mistakes.r: A thermistor's resistance decreases as temperature increases.

mistakes.w: When the thermistor's resistance falls, the p.d. across it rises.
mistakes.r: In a potential divider its share of the p.d. falls; the p.d. across the fixed resistor rises.

mistakes.w: The LDR uses up more voltage in the dark.
mistakes.r: In the dark the LDR has a higher resistance, so it has a larger share of the supply p.d. across it.

mistakes.w: Total resistance of 3 kΩ and 200 Ω in series is 203 Ω.
mistakes.r: Convert units first: 3000 Ω + 200 Ω = 3200 Ω.

mistakes.w: In a sensing circuit the sensor is connected in parallel with the fixed resistor.
mistakes.r: The sensor is in series with the fixed resistor so the supply p.d. is shared between them.

mistakes.w: The LDR detects light by producing a current.
mistakes.r: The LDR's resistance changes; the change in resistance changes the share of p.d. and the current.

exam.q: State what happens to the resistance of an LDR as light intensity increases.
model: Resistance decreases
exam.tip: One word answer, but make sure the direction is right.

exam.q: Give one use of a thermistor.
model: Any one: thermostat / fire alarm / fridge or freezer temperature control / digital thermometer / engine temperature sensor
exam.tip: A specific device scores; 'sensing' alone does not.

exam.q: A 12 Ω resistor and an 18 Ω resistor are connected in series to a 6.0 V battery. Calculate the current.
exam.tip: Find total resistance first, then use I = V ÷ R.

exam.q: Two 10 Ω resistors are connected in parallel. State the total resistance.
model: 5 Ω
exam.tip: Identical resistors in parallel: halve one value.

exam.q: Explain why connecting two resistors in parallel gives a smaller total resistance than either resistor alone.
model: Each resistor has the full supply p.d. across it
Each branch carries a current, so total current is larger than through one resistor alone / extra path for charge
Since R = V ÷ I, a larger current for the same p.d. means a smaller total resistance
exam.tip: Link p.d., current and R = V ÷ I.

exam.q: Explain why the total resistance of two resistors in series is larger than either one.
model: The same current passes through both / charge must go through each in turn
Total p.d. needed is the sum, so R(total) = V ÷ I = R1 + R2 is bigger
exam.tip: Mention one path and that p.d.s add.

exam.q: A thermistor and fixed resistor are in series across a 6 V supply. The output is the p.d. across the fixed resistor. Explain what happens to the output p.d. when the temperature rises.
model: Thermistor resistance decreases as temperature rises
Supply p.d. is shared in the ratio of resistances
So the thermistor has a smaller share of the p.d. / p.d. across thermistor falls
The p.d. across the fixed resistor (output) increases (current increases)
exam.tip: Use the full chain: temperature, resistance, share of p.d., output.

exam.q: In a potential divider, a 4 kΩ fixed resistor is in series with an LDR across 9 V. In the dark the LDR has a resistance of 14 kΩ. Calculate the p.d. across the LDR.
model: R(total) = 4 + 14 = 18 kΩ
exam.tip: Keep everything in kΩ: the units cancel in the ratio.

exam.q: A designer wants a lamp to switch on automatically when it gets dark. Describe how a sensing circuit using an LDR could do this and explain how it works.
model: LDR connected in series with a fixed (or variable) resistor across a supply / potential divider
Output p.d. taken across the LDR, connected to the switch for the lamp
As it gets darker, light intensity falls and the LDR's resistance increases
The LDR then takes a larger share of the supply p.d. (larger R gets larger p.d.)
The output p.d. rises above the switching value and the lamp switches on
A variable resistor allows the light level at which it switches to be adjusted; in bright light the LDR's resistance is low, output low, lamp off
exam.tip: Six-mark answers need the circuit, the sensor behaviour and the p.d. sharing, linked in order.

exam.q: A student finds a total resistance of 24 Ω for an 8 Ω resistor and a 16 Ω resistor in parallel. Explain how you know she has made a mistake.
model: Total resistance in parallel must be less than the smallest resistor (8 Ω)
She has added them, which is only correct for series
exam.tip: Use the 'less than the smallest' check.

worked.q: A 4.0 Ω, a 6.0 Ω and a 10 Ω resistor are in series with a 12 V supply. Find the total resistance, the current and the p.d. across the 10 Ω resistor.
steps: Series: R(total) = 4.0 + 6.0 + 10 = 20 Ω
Same current through each resistor in series

worked.q: Two 12 Ω resistors are in parallel with a 6.0 V battery. Find the current in each, the total current and the total resistance.
steps: Each branch has the full 6.0 V
R(total) = V ÷ I(total) = 6.0 ÷ 1.0 = 6.0 Ω
6.0 Ω is less than 12 Ω, as expected for parallel (half of one identical resistor)
worked.ans: 0.50 A each, 1.0 A total, 6.0 Ω total

worked.q: A thermistor is in series with a 2.0 kΩ fixed resistor across a 6.0 V supply. At 20 °C the thermistor is 4.0 kΩ; at 60 °C it is 1.0 kΩ. Find the p.d. across the fixed resistor at each temperature.
steps: Hotter: thermistor resistance falls, so the fixed resistor's share of p.d. rises
worked.ans: 2.0 V at 20 °C and 4.0 V at 60 °C

phy_ocrb.2.6.summary: When charge flows through a potential difference, energy is transferred: **energy transferred = charge × p.d.** (E = Q × V). **Power** is the rate of energy transfer, so dividing by time and using Q = I × t gives **power = p.d. × current** (P = V × I), and substituting V = I × R gives **power = current² × resistance** (P = I² × R). The I² × R form explains the **heating effect** of a current: doubling the current makes the heating four times larger, which is useful in heaters and kettles but wasteful in wires and cables.

core.p: Potential difference is the energy transferred per coulomb. So if you know how many coulombs pass and how many joules each one transfers, you multiply to get the total energy. This is the starting equation for this point.
bullets: **Energy transferred (J) = charge (C) × potential difference (V)**
E = Q × V (also written W = Q × V, W for work done)
Rearranged: Q = E ÷ V and V = E ÷ Q
Example: 50 C through a 12 V lamp transfers 50 × 12 = 600 J
The energy is transferred **from** the supply **to** the component and then to the surroundings (heating, light)
In the supply the charge gains energy; in the components it transfers energy

callouts.p: energy transferred (joule, J) = charge (coulomb, C) × potential difference (volt, V)

fig.cap: Formula triangles for the two key multiplications on this point. Cover the quantity you want: the other two are either multiplied (side by side) or divided (one above the other). For example, I = P ÷ V and Q = E ÷ V.

core.h: Power: the rate of energy transfer
core.p: Two lamps can transfer the same total energy, but the one that does it faster has a higher power. Power tells you **how many joules are transferred every second**.
bullets: **Power (W) = energy transferred (J) ÷ time (s)**: P = E ÷ t
So E = P × t
1 watt (W) = 1 joule per second (J/s)
1 kilowatt (kW) = 1000 W
A 60 W lamp transfers 60 J every second
A higher-power lamp is brighter because it transfers energy to light (and heat) faster
The **power rating** on an appliance is the power when it is used at its normal p.d.

callouts.p: Power is the rate at which energy is transferred: power = energy transferred ÷ time.

core.p: You can build the electrical power equation from things you already know. This derivation shows why the equation works, and is useful when a question asks you to explain the link between power, p.d. and current.
bullets: Start with E = Q × V
Charge flowing: Q = I × t
Substitute: E = I × t × V = V × I × t
Power: P = E ÷ t = V × I
In words: p.d. is the joules per coulomb; current is the coulombs per second; multiply them and you get **joules per second**, which is watts
Units check: V × A = (J/C) × (C/s) = J/s = W

callouts.p: The power transferred in any circuit device is the p.d. across it multiplied by the current through it: P = V × I.

core.p: This is the most-used power equation. Use the p.d. across, and the current through, the **same component**.
bullets: **Power (W) = potential difference (V) × current (A)**
I = P ÷ V and V = P ÷ I
Kettle: 2300 W on 230 V draws 2300 ÷ 230 = 10 A
Phone charger: 5 V × 2 A = 10 W
For a whole circuit, use the supply p.d. and the current from the supply to get the total power
Power of components adds: total power = sum of the powers of each component (energy is conserved)

callouts.p: Convert kW to W and mA to A before substituting. 3 kW = 3000 W; 250 mA = 0.25 A.

core.h: Deriving and using P = I² × R
core.p: If you know the current and the resistance but not the p.d., combine P = V × I with V = I × R. This form is especially useful for the energy wasted in wires, where you know the current and the wire resistance.
bullets: P = V × I and V = I × R
So P = (I × R) × I = **I² × R**
**Power (W) = current² (A²) × resistance (Ω)**
Rearranged: R = P ÷ I² and I = square root of (P ÷ R)
Square the current **before** multiplying by R
Example: 3 A in a 10 Ω resistor: P = 3² × 10 = 9 × 10 = 90 W

callouts.p: power (W) = current² (A²) × resistance (Ω)
3 × 3 × 10 = 90, not 3 × 10 = 30 and not (3 × 10)² = 900. Only the current is squared.

core.p: For a fixed resistor, the power depends on the **square** of the current. Doubling the current doubles the p.d. needed (V = IR), and twice the current at twice the p.d. means 2 × 2 = 4 times the power. This is why small increases in current can cause large increases in heating.
bullets: Double I: power × 4
Triple I: power × 9
Halve I: power ÷ 4
Graph of P against I for a fixed resistor is a **curve (parabola)** through the origin, getting steeper
Graph of P against I² would be a straight line through the origin with gradient R
This idea explains why the National Grid transmits at low current (covered in the next point)

core.h: The heating effect of a current
core.p: In a metal, the current is a flow of free electrons drifting between the positive metal ions of the lattice. The electrons keep colliding with the ions, transferring energy to them. The ions vibrate more, which means the metal's **thermal energy store** increases and it gets hotter. This is the physical reason for resistance and for the I² × R heating.
bullets: Free electrons are accelerated by the p.d. and gain kinetic energy
They **collide with the vibrating positive ions** in the metal lattice
Energy is transferred to the ions: they vibrate more, so the temperature rises
More current means more electrons per second and more collisions per second, so more heating
Energy is then transferred to the surroundings by heating (and light, for a hot filament)
A higher temperature makes ions vibrate more, so resistance of a metal rises as it heats up

callouts.p: Electrons collide with ions; ions vibrate more; temperature of the wire increases.

fig.cap: Inside a metal wire. Free electrons drift through a lattice of positive metal ions and keep colliding with them. Each collision transfers energy to the ions, which vibrate more, so the wire heats up. This is why current produces a heating effect.

core.p: The heating effect is sometimes exactly what we want and sometimes energy wasted. Engineers choose resistance and current to maximise useful power or minimise waste.
bullets: **Useful**: electric heaters, kettles, toasters, hair dryers, immersion heaters, ovens, filament lamps (to make the filament glow)
**Fuses**: a thin wire that heats and melts if the current gets too high, breaking the circuit
**Wasteful**: heating of connecting wires, cables, chargers, motors and computers
Thick copper cables have low resistance, so I² × R in them is small
Long-distance cables use low current so that I² × R losses are small
Wasted energy reduces the efficiency of a device

core.p: Many questions are really a test of picking the equation that matches the data you are given. List what you know and what you want, then choose.
bullets: Given Q and V, want energy: E = Q × V
Given I and t, want charge: Q = I × t
Given V and I, want power: P = V × I
Given I and R, want power: P = I² × R
Given P and t, want energy: E = P × t
Given V and R, want I: I = V ÷ R, then use P = V × I
Multi-step questions often chain two of these

callouts.p: Write the equation, substitute with units, calculate, then give units. Method marks are awarded even if the final answer is wrong.

core.h: Energy over time and paying for electricity
core.p: Appliances transfer energy at a steady rate, so the energy used depends on both power and time. Domestic energy is often measured in kilowatt-hours to keep the numbers manageable.
bullets: E = P × t with P in W and t in s gives energy in J
E = P × t with P in kW and t in hours gives energy in **kilowatt-hours (kWh)**
Cost = energy used (kWh) × price per kWh
A 2 kW heater for 3 hours uses 6 kWh
Leaving low-power devices on for a long time can still use a lot of energy

callouts.p: In E = P × t with watts, time must be in seconds. 5 minutes = 300 s.

core.h: Power in series and parallel circuits
core.p: Combining this point with the circuit rules lets you compare how bright lamps are. Brightness depends on the power of the lamp, which depends on both the p.d. across it and the current through it.
bullets: Series: same current, so the component with the **larger resistance** has the larger power (P = I² × R)
Parallel: same p.d., so the branch with the **smaller resistance** draws more current and has the larger power (P = V × I)
Two identical lamps in series on 6 V: each gets 3 V and half the current, so each has a quarter of the power it would have alone
Total power from the supply = supply p.d. × total current = sum of component powers

analogy.t: Delivery vans and parcels of energy
analogy.p: Imagine each coulomb of charge is a delivery van, and the p.d. is how many joules of parcels each van drops off at a component. Total energy delivered is number of vans × parcels per van: E = Q × V. The current is how many vans arrive every second, so the rate of delivery (power) is vans per second × parcels per van: P = I × V. The heating effect is like the vans bumping into bollards (ions) along a narrow street: twice as many vans per second, each pushed twice as hard, makes four times as much bumping, which is I² × R. Where it breaks down: real charges are not used up or emptied like vans; the same electrons keep circulating, and the energy is carried by the electric field in the circuit, not literally inside each electron.

terms.d: Energy moved from one store to another by the electric current; energy = charge × p.d.; measured in joules (J).
Energy transferred by a force; in circuits, energy transferred as charge moves through a p.d.
Amount of electricity flowing; measured in coulombs (C); Q = I × t.
Energy transferred per unit charge between two points; measured in volts (V).
Rate of flow of charge; measured in amperes (A).
P.d. divided by current; measured in ohms (Ω).
Rate of energy transfer; P = E ÷ t; measured in watts (W).
Unit of power; 1 W = 1 joule per second.
1000 watts.
Energy transferred by a 1 kW appliance in 1 hour; equal to 3.6 million joules.
The power of an appliance when used at its normal operating p.d.
Temperature rise of a conductor carrying current, caused by electrons colliding with ions; power = I² × R.
Regular arrangement of positive metal ions in a metal, through which free electrons move.
Electrons in a metal that are not bound to one atom and can move to carry a current.
Thin wire that melts when the current is too high, breaking the circuit; relies on the heating effect.
Useful energy (or power) output ÷ total energy (or power) input.

mistakes.w: P = I × R²
mistakes.r: P = I² × R: it is the current that is squared, not the resistance.

mistakes.w: Power = 3 × 10 = 30 W for 3 A in 10 Ω.
mistakes.r: P = I² × R = 3² × 10 = 90 W; square the current first.

mistakes.w: Power is the amount of energy used.
mistakes.r: Power is the rate of energy transfer (energy transferred per second).

mistakes.w: E = Q × V with time in minutes / P = E ÷ t with t = 5 for 5 minutes.
mistakes.r: Time must be in seconds: 5 minutes = 300 s.

mistakes.w: 1 watt is 1 joule per coulomb.
mistakes.r: 1 watt is 1 joule per second; 1 joule per coulomb is 1 volt.

mistakes.w: Doubling the current doubles the heating in a resistor.
mistakes.r: P = I² × R, so doubling the current makes the power four times bigger.

mistakes.w: The wire gets hot because electrons rub against each other / friction.
mistakes.r: Electrons collide with the positive ions in the metal lattice, making the ions vibrate more, so the temperature rises.

mistakes.w: The current is used up to make heat.
mistakes.r: Energy is transferred to the thermal store; the current is the same in and out of the component.

mistakes.w: Uses the supply p.d. with the current in one branch to get that branch's power and then adds wrong values.
mistakes.r: Use the p.d. across and current through the same component; then total power = sum of component powers.

exam.q: State the unit of power.
model: watt (W) / joule per second
exam.tip: Do not write 'volt' or 'joule'.

exam.q: Write down the equation that links energy transferred, charge and potential difference.
model: energy transferred = charge × potential difference (E = QV)
exam.tip: Words or standard symbols both score.

exam.q: A charge of 30 C passes through a lamp with a p.d. of 6.0 V across it. Calculate the energy transferred.
exam.tip: Unit J is needed for the final mark.

exam.q: A kettle connected to 230 V draws a current of 12 A. Calculate its power in kW.
exam.tip: Read the unit asked for and convert at the end.

exam.q: A current of 0.50 A flows through a 40 Ω resistor. Calculate the power transferred.
Show that the equation P = V × I can be written as P = I² × R.
model: V = I × R
substitute: P = (I × R) × I = I² × R
exam.tip: Show the substitution step clearly.

exam.q: The current in a heating element is doubled while its resistance stays the same. State and explain what happens to its power.
model: Power becomes four times bigger
Because P = I² × R / power is proportional to current squared
exam.tip: Quote the equation as your reason.

exam.q: A 2.0 kW heater is switched on for 15 minutes. Calculate the energy transferred in joules.
exam.tip: Two conversions: kW to W, minutes to seconds.

exam.q: A 12 V lamp is rated at 36 W. Calculate the current and the resistance of the lamp when it is working normally.
exam.tip: Use your first answer to get the second; carry the unit through.

exam.q: Explain, in terms of electrons and ions, why a metal wire gets hot when a current flows through it, and why the heating increases sharply when the current increases.
model: Current is a flow of free electrons through the metal lattice
The electrons collide with the positive metal ions
Energy is transferred to the ions, which vibrate more
So the temperature of the wire / its thermal store increases
A bigger current means more electrons per second and more collisions, transferring energy faster
Power = I² × R, so doubling the current gives four times the heating power
exam.tip: Combine the particle explanation with the equation for full marks.

worked.q: A torch lamp has a p.d. of 3.0 V across it and carries a current of 0.20 A for 10 minutes. Calculate (a) the charge that flows and (b) the energy transferred.
steps: Convert time: 10 minutes = 600 s
Check with power: P = V × I = 3.0 × 0.20 = 0.60 W; E = P × t = 0.60 × 600 = 360 J

worked.q: A 6.0 Ω resistor carries a current of 2.0 A. The current is increased to 4.0 A. Calculate the power before and after, and the ratio.
steps: Doubling the current made the power four times bigger, as expected from I²
worked.ans: 24 W before, 96 W after; power increases by a factor of 4

worked.q: An electric shower is rated 9.2 kW on a 230 V supply. Find the current it draws and the energy it transfers in a 6 minute shower.
steps: In kWh: 9.2 kW × 0.1 h = 0.92 kWh

phy_ocrb.2.7.summary: A **transformer** is two coils of wire wound on a soft iron core; it changes the size of an **alternating** potential difference. A **step-up** transformer increases the p.d. and a **step-down** transformer decreases it, and for a 100% efficient transformer **power in = power out**, so Vp × Ip = Vs × Is: raising the p.d. lowers the current. The National Grid steps the p.d. up to hundreds of kilovolts for transmission because, for the same power, a lower current means much smaller **I² × R heating losses** in the cables, then steps it down to a safe 230 V for homes.

core.p: A transformer is a device that changes an alternating potential difference from one value to another. It has no moving parts. It is made of two separate coils of insulated wire wound around the same **soft iron core**. The coils are not electrically connected to each other; energy is passed from one to the other through the changing magnetism of the core.
bullets: **Primary coil**: the input coil, connected to the a.c. supply
**Secondary coil**: the output coil, connected to the load
**Soft iron core**: links the two coils magnetically; iron is easily magnetised and demagnetised
The coils are made of insulated copper wire so current goes round the turns, not across them
No wire connects the primary to the secondary
Transformers only work with **alternating current (a.c.)**, not direct current (d.c.)

callouts.p: A device made of two coils wound on an iron core that changes the size of an alternating potential difference.

fig.cap: Structure of a transformer. The a.c. input goes to the primary coil on the left; the output is taken from the secondary coil on the right. Both coils are wound on the same soft iron core but are not connected by any wire. This one is a step-up transformer: the secondary has more turns, so the output p.d. is higher than the input p.d.

core.p: An alternating current in the primary coil produces a magnetic field in the iron core that keeps changing in size and direction. This changing magnetic field passes through the secondary coil and induces an alternating p.d. across it. A steady d.c. would make a steady field, and a steady field induces nothing, so a transformer cannot work with d.c.
bullets: a.c. in primary gives a **changing magnetic field** in the core
The core carries this changing field to the secondary coil
The changing field **induces** an alternating p.d. in the secondary
d.c. gives a constant field: **no** p.d. is induced (except briefly when switched on or off)
This is one reason mains electricity is a.c.
UK mains supply: **230 V a.c., 50 Hz**

callouts.p: A transformer only produces an output when the magnetic field in the core is changing, which is why it needs a.c.

core.p: Transformers are named by what they do to the p.d. A step-up transformer makes the output p.d. bigger than the input; a step-down transformer makes it smaller. You cannot get something for nothing: if the p.d. goes up, the current must go down, because the power cannot increase.
bullets: **Step-up**: output (secondary) p.d. is **greater** than input (primary) p.d.; secondary has more turns
**Step-down**: output p.d. is **less** than input p.d.; secondary has fewer turns
Step-up: current is **decreased** on the output side
Step-down: current is **increased** on the output side
Examples of step-down: phone chargers, laptop power supplies, doorbells, substations near homes
Example of step-up: at power stations, to feed the National Grid

core.p: Energy is conserved, so a transformer cannot output more power than it receives. Real transformers are very efficient (often above 95%), so at GCSE we assume they are **100% efficient**. Then the input power equals the output power, and since power = p.d. × current, you get the transformer power equation.
bullets: Input power = Vp × Ip; output power = Vs × Is
**Vp × Ip = Vs × Is** (for a 100% efficient transformer)
Vp = p.d. across primary, Ip = current in primary
Vs = p.d. across secondary, Is = current in secondary
If the p.d. is multiplied by a factor, the current is divided by the same factor
Rearranging: Is = (Vp × Ip) ÷ Vs

callouts.p: potential difference across primary coil × current in primary coil = potential difference across secondary coil × current in secondary coil
A step-up transformer increases the p.d. but NOT the power or the energy. The current goes down to compensate.

fig.cap: Power in equals power out in an ideal step-down transformer. 230 V × 0.50 A = 115 W goes in and 11.5 V × 10 A = 115 W comes out. The p.d. has been reduced 20 times, so the current has increased 20 times.

core.p: Real transformers are not quite 100% efficient. Some energy is transferred to the thermal store of the transformer itself, which is why large ones have cooling fins or oil, and chargers feel warm.
bullets: Heating of the coils by the current (I² × R in the copper wire)
Heating of the iron core as it is magnetised and demagnetised
Losses are kept small by using low-resistance copper coils and a soft iron core
Efficiency = useful power output ÷ total power input
In real transformers Vs × Is is slightly less than Vp × Ip

core.p: The National Grid is the network of cables, pylons and transformers that connects power stations to homes, schools and businesses across the country. Generators produce a.c. at around 25 kV. Step-up transformers raise this to very high p.d.s, typically 275 kV or 400 kV, for the long-distance cables. Near towns, step-down transformers at substations reduce the p.d. in stages, until it reaches 230 V for homes.
bullets: Power stations generate a.c. at about **25 kV**
**Step-up transformer** raises the p.d. to **275 kV or 400 kV** for transmission
Overhead cables on pylons (or underground cables) carry the energy long distances
**Step-down transformers** at substations lower the p.d. in stages
Homes receive **230 V**; some factories take a higher p.d.
The Grid lets energy be moved from where it is generated to where it is needed and lets supply be matched to demand

callouts.p: power station, step-up transformer, transmission cables, step-down transformer, consumer.

core.h: Why high-voltage transmission is more efficient
core.p: The cables carrying energy across the country have resistance, so a current in them heats them up and wastes energy. The power wasted is P = I² × R. For a given power to be delivered, P = V × I, so if the transmission p.d. is made much larger, the current needed is much smaller. Because the loss depends on **current squared**, cutting the current cuts the loss dramatically.
bullets: Power to transmit is fixed by demand: P = V × I
**Higher p.d. means lower current** for the same power
Heating loss in cables = **I² × R**
**Lower current means much less energy lost** by heating the cables
Reduce current 10 times: loss falls 100 times
Less energy wasted, so the Grid is **more efficient** and more of the generated power reaches consumers
Lower current also allows thinner, lighter, cheaper cables and pylons spaced further apart

callouts.p: Step-up increases p.d.; so current decreases (P = VI, same power); heating loss is I²R; so less energy is wasted / more efficient.
Do not say high voltage 'reduces resistance'. The cable resistance is the same; it is the current that falls.

fig.cap: Power lost as heat in 10 Ω of cable when 100 MW is transmitted at different p.d.s. At 50 kV the current is 2000 A and 40 MW is lost; at 400 kV the current is only 250 A and about 0.6 MW is lost. Doubling the p.d. halves the current and quarters the loss.

core.p: Very high p.d.s are extremely dangerous: they can push a large current through a person and can make sparks jump across air gaps. So they are kept far from people on tall pylons with insulators, and stepped down before reaching homes.
bullets: 400 kV would be lethal and impossible to insulate safely inside houses
Domestic appliances are designed to work on 230 V
Pylons are tall so the cables are well above people, vehicles and trees
Cables are hung from **insulators** so current does not flow into the pylon
Underground cables are used in some places but are more expensive to install and repair
Step-down is done in stages: 400 kV, then 132 kV, 33 kV, 11 kV and finally 230 V

core.p: Engineers choose transmission p.d.s by weighing up efficiency against cost and safety. Questions may ask you to evaluate these.
bullets: Benefit: much less energy wasted in cables, so less fuel burned and lower emissions for the same energy delivered
Benefit: thinner cables, so less copper or aluminium and lighter pylons
Cost: transformers and substations are expensive to build and maintain
Cost: very high p.d. needs large insulators, tall pylons and safety zones
Some people object to the visual impact of pylons
Overall, for long distances, high-voltage transmission saves far more than it costs

core.h: Calculating with transformers and cable losses
core.p: Typical calculations ask for the current on one side of a transformer, or for how much power is lost in a cable at different p.d.s. Use the power equation first, then I² × R.
bullets: Step 1: find the current: I = P ÷ V
Step 2: find the cable loss: P(loss) = I² × R(cable)
Step 3 (optional): efficiency = (P - P(loss)) ÷ P × 100%
Transformer current: Is = Vp × Ip ÷ Vs
Check: in a step-up transformer the secondary current must come out smaller than the primary current

callouts.p: Convert kV to V (× 1000) and MW to W (× 1 000 000) before calculating, or the current will be wrong by large factors.

analogy.t: Moving water through a long hose
analogy.p: Imagine you need to deliver a fixed amount of water power to a distant garden through a long, narrow hose that wastes energy by rubbing (friction) against the water. You could send a huge flow of water at low pressure, but the big flow rubs a lot and wastes energy. Or you could use a pump to push a small flow at very high pressure, which delivers the same power with far less rubbing. The pump at the start is the step-up transformer, high pressure is high p.d., the small flow is low current, and the friction loss is I² × R. At the house a valve reduces the pressure back to a safe level (step-down transformer). Where it breaks down: water is actually carried from one end to the other, whereas in a.c. transmission the electrons just jiggle back and forth and the energy is carried by the electric and magnetic fields; also a hose pump works with steady flow, but a transformer only works with alternating current.

terms.d: Device with two coils on an iron core that changes the size of an alternating p.d.
The input coil of a transformer, connected to the a.c. supply.
The output coil of a transformer, connected to the load.
Core that links the two coils; easily magnetised and demagnetised so it carries the changing magnetic field.
Transformer whose output p.d. is greater than its input p.d. (and output current smaller).
Transformer whose output p.d. is less than its input p.d. (and output current greater).
Current that repeatedly changes direction; UK mains is 230 V at 50 Hz.
Current that flows in one direction only, such as from a cell; cannot be used with a transformer.
Network of cables and transformers linking power stations to consumers across the country.
Long-distance cables, usually overhead on pylons, carrying electricity at high p.d.
Site where step-down transformers reduce the p.d. before distribution to consumers.
Energy per second wasted by heating cables; equal to I² × R.
Useful power output ÷ total power input; higher when less energy is wasted.
Power in equals power out for a 100% efficient transformer.
Non-conducting support that stops current flowing from the cable into the pylon.
1000 volts; transmission p.d.s are 275 kV or 400 kV.

mistakes.w: A step-up transformer increases the power.
mistakes.r: It increases the p.d. but decreases the current; power out is at most equal to power in (energy is conserved).

mistakes.w: High voltage is used because it travels faster / further.
mistakes.r: High p.d. means low current for the same power, so less energy is lost by heating the cables (I²R).

mistakes.w: High voltage reduces the resistance of the cables.
mistakes.r: The cable resistance is unchanged; the current is reduced, so I²R heating is reduced.

mistakes.w: Transformers work with batteries / d.c.
mistakes.r: Transformers only work with a.c., because a changing magnetic field is needed to induce a p.d. in the secondary.

mistakes.w: The current flows through the iron core from one coil to the other.
mistakes.r: The coils are not electrically connected; a changing magnetic field in the core induces a p.d. in the secondary.

mistakes.w: Step-down transformers are used at power stations.
mistakes.r: Step-up at power stations, step-down at substations near consumers.

mistakes.w: Less current means less energy is lost, so halving current halves the loss.
mistakes.r: Loss = I²R, so halving the current makes the loss four times smaller.

mistakes.w: The p.d. is stepped down because homes cannot use so much energy.
mistakes.r: It is stepped down for safety and because appliances are designed for 230 V.

exam.q: Name the part of a transformer that links the two coils.
model: (soft) iron core
exam.tip: Say 'iron', not just 'metal'.

exam.q: State the type of transformer used at a power station to connect to the National Grid.
model: step-up transformer
exam.tip: Power station end: up; home end: down.

exam.q: Explain why a transformer will not work with a direct current supply.
model: d.c. produces a constant / unchanging magnetic field in the core
A changing magnetic field is needed to induce a p.d. in the secondary coil
exam.tip: Key word: changing.

exam.q: An ideal transformer has 230 V across the primary and a current of 0.20 A. The secondary p.d. is 11.5 V. Calculate the secondary current.
model: Vp × Ip = Vs × Is
exam.tip: Work out the power first (46 W), then divide by Vs.

exam.q: State what happens to the current when a transformer steps up the p.d., and explain why.
model: Current decreases
Power in = power out / Vp × Ip = Vs × Is, so if V increases I must decrease
exam.tip: Use conservation of energy as the reason.

exam.q: Power of 500 kW is transmitted through cables of total resistance 4.0 Ω. Calculate the power lost in the cables when the p.d. is (a) 10 kV and (b) 100 kV.
exam.tip: Ten times the p.d. gives one hundredth of the loss.

exam.q: Explain why the National Grid transmits electricity at very high potential difference.
model: For the same power, a higher p.d. means a lower current (P = V × I)
Power lost in the cables by heating = I² × R
So a lower current means much less energy wasted as heat in the cables
So transmission is more efficient / more energy reaches consumers / thinner cables can be used
exam.tip: The examiner wants the link from p.d. to current to heating loss.

exam.q: Give one reason why the p.d. is stepped down before it reaches homes.
model: Very high p.d. is dangerous / appliances are designed for 230 V
exam.tip: Safety is the usual answer.

exam.q: Describe the structure of a transformer and how it changes an alternating p.d.
model: Two coils of insulated wire, primary and secondary
Wound on a soft iron core; coils not electrically connected
a.c. in the primary produces a changing magnetic field in the core
The changing field induces an alternating p.d. in the secondary (more turns gives a bigger p.d. for step-up)
exam.tip: Structure first, then the sequence of how it works.

exam.q: Describe how electricity gets from a power station to a home and explain the role of transformers in making the system efficient and safe.
model: Generator produces a.c. at about 25 kV
Step-up transformer increases p.d. to about 400 kV (or 275 kV)
This reduces the current for the same power (Vp × Ip = Vs × Is)
Lower current means less I² × R heating in the transmission cables, so less energy is wasted / more efficient
Step-down transformers at substations reduce the p.d. (in stages) to 230 V
Low p.d. is safer for use in homes; high p.d. cables are kept on tall pylons with insulators
exam.tip: Cover the route in order, then the efficiency reason, then safety.

worked.q: A phone charger contains a step-down transformer. The input is 230 V and 0.025 A. The output p.d. is 5.0 V. Assuming 100% efficiency, find the output current.
steps: Power in = Vp × Ip = 230 × 0.025 = 5.75 W
Power out = power in = 5.75 W
Check: p.d. went down (230 V to 5 V) so the current should go up: 0.025 A to 1.15 A
worked.ans: 1.15 A (about 1.2 A)

worked.q: A town needs 2.0 MW. The cables between the power station and the town have a total resistance of 5.0 Ω. Compare the power lost if it is sent at 20 kV and at 400 kV.
steps: The p.d. is 20 times higher, so the current is 20 times lower and the loss is 20² = 400 times lower
worked.ans: 50 kW lost at 20 kV; 125 W lost at 400 kV (400 times less)

worked.q: Explain in a model answer why a step-up transformer is used at a power station.
steps: The step-up transformer increases the p.d. of the electricity sent into the transmission cables
The power delivered stays the same, so by P = V × I the current in the cables is reduced
The heating of the cables depends on I² × R
A much smaller current therefore wastes much less energy heating the cables
So more of the generated energy reaches consumers and the Grid is more efficient
worked.ans: Higher p.d. gives lower current for the same power, so I² × R losses in the cables are much smaller and transmission is more efficient.

phy_ocrb.2.8.summary: A magnet has a north and a south pole and is surrounded by a **magnetic field**, the region where another magnet or a magnetic material (iron, steel, nickel, cobalt) feels a non-contact force. **Like poles repel and unlike poles attract**; a **permanent magnet** makes its own field all the time, while an **induced magnet** is only magnetic while it sits in another field and is always attracted. Field lines show both the direction (N to S) and the strength (closeness of lines) of a field, and the way a compass behaves anywhere on Earth is evidence that the Earth's core is magnetic.

core.h: Magnetic poles and the forces between them
core.p: Every magnet has two **poles**, called north-seeking (N) and south-seeking (S). The poles are where the magnetic force is strongest. When two magnets are brought close, they exert a **non-contact force** on each other: the force acts across a gap, without touching, because each magnet sits in the other's field.
bullets: **Like poles repel**: N and N push apart, S and S push apart.
**Unlike poles attract**: N and S pull together.
The force is **stronger when the poles are closer** together and weaker as they move apart.
The forces on the two magnets are **equal in size and opposite in direction** (a Newton's third law pair).
Magnetic poles always come in pairs: cut a bar magnet in half and you get two smaller magnets, each with N and S.

callouts.p: Like poles repel, unlike poles attract. This is the only way to be sure an object is a magnet: test for **repulsion**.

fig.cap: Top: a south pole facing a north pole. Field lines run straight across the gap from N to S and the magnets attract (green force arrows). Bottom: two south poles facing. Lines bend away from each other, there is a neutral point X where the fields cancel, and the magnets repel (red force arrows).

core.p: Only a few materials are affected by magnets. These **magnetic materials** are attracted to either pole of a magnet. Most metals, such as copper, aluminium, gold and silver, are not magnetic at all.
bullets: The magnetic elements to learn are **iron, nickel and cobalt**, plus alloys of them such as **steel** (mainly iron).
A magnetic material is **always attracted** to a magnet, never repelled, whichever pole is used.
Non-magnetic materials (copper, aluminium, plastic, wood, glass) feel no force.
A steel can is attracted to a magnet; an aluminium can is not, which is how recycling centres separate them.

head: Material
Magnetic?
Notes
rows: Magnetised easily, loses it easily: used for induced magnets and electromagnet cores
Harder to magnetise but keeps its magnetism: used for permanent magnets
Magnetic elements, used in magnet alloys

callouts.p: Do not write that metals are attracted to magnets. Only iron, nickel, cobalt and their alloys (such as steel) are.

core.p: A **permanent magnet** produces its own magnetic field all the time. An **induced magnet** is a piece of magnetic material that becomes a magnet only when it is placed in a magnetic field. When the field is taken away, an induced magnet loses most or all of its magnetism quickly.
bullets: Permanent magnets are usually made of **steel** or special alloys; they can attract or repel.
Induced magnetism is why an iron nail or paper clip sticks to a magnet: the magnet first turns it into a temporary magnet.
The end of the material nearest the magnet becomes the **opposite pole**, so the force between a magnet and an induced magnet is **always attraction**.
You can hang a chain of paper clips from a magnet: each clip is magnetised by induction and attracts the next one; take the magnet away and the chain falls apart.
**Soft iron** is used where we want a magnet that can be switched on and off, because it gains and loses induced magnetism easily.

head: Permanent magnet
Induced magnet
rows: Has its own field all the time
Only magnetic while in another field

callouts.p: A material that becomes a magnet when it is placed in a magnetic field. It loses most or all of its magnetism when removed from the field.

fig.cap: Induced magnetism. The iron nail becomes a magnet only while it is in the field of the permanent magnet. The end nearest the N pole becomes an induced S pole, so the nail is attracted. Remove the magnet and soft iron loses almost all its magnetism.

core.p: A **magnetic field** is the region around a magnet where a force acts on another magnet or on a magnetic material. It is invisible, but we can map its shape and direction using iron filings or plotting compasses.
bullets: The field is strongest **at the poles** and gets **weaker with distance** from the magnet.
The **direction** of the field at any point is the direction of the force on a north pole placed there.
So the field direction points **away from N and towards S**.
A magnetic field is a vector field: at each point it has a size (strength) and a direction, and both change from point to point.

callouts.p: The region around a magnet where a force acts on another magnet or on a magnetic material.
The direction of the force that would act on a north pole placed at that point; this is the direction a compass needle's N end points.

core.p: We show a field using **magnetic field lines** (lines of force). The pattern of lines shows two things at once: the arrows show the **direction** at each point, and the **spacing** shows the **strength**.
bullets: Lines go **from the N pole to the S pole** outside the magnet; always draw arrows on them.
Lines **never cross**: the field can only have one direction at any point.
**Closer lines mean a stronger field**: lines are packed together at the poles and spread out further away.
Lines start and end on the magnet; they leave the N pole and enter the S pole at right angles to the end faces.
The direction of the field changes from point to point: next to the side of a bar magnet the field runs parallel to the magnet, back towards the S end.
Between unlike poles facing each other the lines are straight, parallel and evenly spaced: this region is a **uniform field**.

callouts.p: Usually 3 marks: correct shape, arrows from N to S on every line, and lines closer together at the poles. Use a sharp pencil and make lines smooth and non-crossing.

fig.cap: Field around a bar magnet. Field lines leave the north pole and enter the south pole, so the arrows point from N to S outside the magnet. The lines are closest together at the poles, where the field is strongest, and spread out with distance, where the field is weaker. Field lines never cross.

core.h: Plotting a field with a compass
core.p: A **plotting compass** is a tiny magnet (needle) free to turn. It lines up with the magnetic field, with its N end pointing in the field direction. This lets you trace the field lines around a magnet step by step.
bullets: Place the bar magnet on paper and draw round it.
Put the compass near one pole and mark a dot at the point the **N end of the needle** points to.
Move the compass so the **tail** of the needle is over the dot, and mark a new dot at its tip.
Repeat until you reach the other pole, then join the dots with a smooth curve and add an arrow (N to S).
Start from several different points near the pole to build up the whole pattern.
**Iron filings** sprinkled on paper over a magnet show the shape quickly but **not the direction**; a compass shows the direction.

callouts.p: Keep other magnets, steel rulers and iron objects away. The Earth's own field also affects the compass far from the magnet, where the magnet's field is weak.

fig.cap: Plotting a field line with a small plotting compass. Put the compass near the N pole, mark a dot at the end its north (red) needle points to, move the compass so its tail sits on that dot, and repeat until you reach the S pole. Joining the dots gives one field line; the needle always lines up along the field.

core.h: How field strength and direction change from point to point
core.p: The spec asks you to describe how strength and direction change around a magnet. Think of moving a compass around the magnet and watching the needle.
bullets: Near a pole the field is **strong** and points straight out of N (or straight into S).
Moving away from the magnet the lines spread out, so the field gets **weaker**; far away a compass is dominated by the Earth's field.
Moving around the magnet, the needle turns smoothly: the **direction changes continuously** along each curved line.
At the middle of the side of a bar magnet the field is parallel to the magnet, pointing from the N end towards the S end.
A compass needle turns right round (through 360 degrees) as it is carried once around the magnet.

callouts.p: You cannot read strength from a single line. Strength is shown by how closely the lines are spaced in that region.

core.p: A compass needle is a small **permanent magnet** on a pivot. Forces from a magnetic field act on its two poles and turn it until it lies **along the field line** at that point. If there are no nearby magnets, it lines up with the Earth's magnetic field.
bullets: The N end of the needle is pushed in the field direction and the S end the opposite way, so the needle rotates.
It stops when it points along the field, with N in the field direction.
A compass is a **field detector**: if the needle swings when you bring something near, that object has a magnetic field or is magnetic.

core.p: The Earth has its own magnetic field, shaped like the field of a giant bar magnet. A freely suspended magnet or a compass anywhere on Earth settles pointing roughly north-south. This behaviour is the evidence that the **Earth's core is magnetic**.
bullets: A compass needle points towards **geographic north** wherever you are on the Earth's surface.
Because the N end of a compass is attracted to it, the pole in the Arctic must be a **magnetic south pole**.
Field lines come out of the Earth near the geographic South Pole and go in near the geographic North Pole.
The magnetic poles are **close to, but not exactly at**, the geographic poles.
The pattern of the Earth's field matches the field of a bar magnet, so scientists conclude the Earth contains a magnetic core.
The core is mainly iron and nickel; its magnetism produces the field we detect at the surface.

callouts.p: Compasses everywhere on Earth line up with a field shaped like a bar magnet's field. This is evidence that the Earth has a magnetic core.

fig.cap: The Earth behaves as if it had a huge bar magnet inside it. Field lines leave near the geographic South Pole and enter near the geographic North Pole, so the pole in the Arctic is really a magnetic south pole. A compass needle lines up with the field, so its N end points to geographic north.

core.h: Using compasses as evidence for a magnetic core
core.p: OCR likes questions that ask how observations support a model. Here the observation is compass behaviour and the model is a magnetic core.
bullets: Observation 1: a compass always settles pointing north-south, so there must be a magnetic field all over the Earth's surface.
Observation 2: compasses at different places point along lines that run from the southern hemisphere to the northern hemisphere, the same pattern as around a bar magnet.
Observation 3: a suspended compass needle also dips at an angle towards the ground in many places, showing the field lines go into and out of the Earth.
Conclusion: the field is produced inside the Earth, so the **core must be magnetic**.
Without the magnetic core, a compass would not line up in any particular direction.

callouts.p: Use a chain: compass is a magnet, it lines up with a magnetic field, it lines up the same way all over the Earth, so the Earth must have a magnetic field, so its core is magnetic.

core.h: Uses of permanent and induced magnets
core.p: Knowing which kind of magnet to use comes down to whether you need the magnetism to stay or to be switched off.
bullets: Permanent magnets: fridge door seals, compasses, loudspeakers, microphones, electric motors and generators.
Induced magnets: the soft iron core of an electromagnet, scrap-yard cranes, relays and magnetic door locks.
Magnetic separators in recycling plants use magnets to pull steel (iron) cans away from aluminium cans.
Magnetic materials are used in older data storage, such as hard drives and magnetic strips on cards.

analogy.t: Field lines are like traffic on one-way roads
analogy.p: Imagine a town map where cars always drive out of the north car park and into the south car park, on one-way roads that never cross. Where roads are bunched together, traffic is heavy (strong field); out in the countryside the roads are far apart (weak field). A compass is like a car that always faces along the road it is on. The analogy breaks down because nothing actually flows along a magnetic field line: the lines are a way of picturing the direction and strength of a force, not a path that something travels along.

terms.d: A region at the end of a magnet where the magnetic force is strongest; either north-seeking or south-seeking.
The region around a magnet where a force acts on another magnet or on a magnetic material.
A line showing the direction of the magnetic field; it points from N to S, and the closer the lines the stronger the field.
The direction of the force on a north pole placed at that point.
A magnet that produces its own magnetic field all the time.
A material that becomes a magnet when placed in a magnetic field and loses most or all of its magnetism when removed.
A material attracted by a magnet: iron, nickel, cobalt and alloys such as steel.
A force that acts between objects that are not touching, such as the magnetic force.
A pushing apart between like poles; the only reliable test that an object is a magnet.
A pulling together, between unlike poles or between a magnet and a magnetic material.
A small compass used to find the direction of a magnetic field at a point and to trace field lines.
A field with the same strength and direction everywhere, shown by straight, parallel, equally spaced lines.
Iron that is easily magnetised and easily loses its magnetism; used for induced magnets.
The field around the Earth, shaped like a bar magnet's field, caused by its magnetic core.
A point between magnets where their fields cancel, so there is no resultant field.

mistakes.w: All metals are magnetic.
mistakes.r: Only iron, nickel, cobalt and their alloys (such as steel) are magnetic; copper and aluminium are not.

mistakes.w: Field lines go from S to N.
mistakes.r: Outside a magnet, field lines point from the north pole to the south pole.

mistakes.w: Field lines touch or cross where the field is strong.
mistakes.r: Field lines never cross; a strong field is shown by lines that are closer together.

mistakes.w: Attraction proves an object is a magnet.
mistakes.r: A magnetic material is also attracted; only repulsion proves the object is a permanent magnet.

mistakes.w: An induced magnet can be repelled by a magnet.
mistakes.r: The force between a magnet and an induced magnet is always attraction, because the nearest end becomes the opposite pole.

mistakes.w: The Earth's North Pole is a magnetic north pole.
mistakes.r: The compass N end is attracted to it, so near the geographic North Pole there is a magnetic south pole.

mistakes.w: Iron filings show the direction of the field.
mistakes.r: Iron filings show the shape of the field only; a plotting compass shows its direction.

mistakes.w: An induced magnet stays magnetic forever.
mistakes.r: An induced magnet loses most or all of its magnetism when it is removed from the field.

mistakes.w: A compass points to the North Pole because the North Pole attracts metal.
mistakes.r: The compass needle is a magnet that lines up with the Earth's magnetic field, which comes from the magnetic core.

exam.q: State what happens when the north pole of one magnet is brought close to the north pole of another.
model: They repel (push apart).
exam.tip: One word answers are fine for 1 mark, but repel must be spelt clearly.

exam.q: Name two magnetic elements.
model: Any two from iron, nickel, cobalt (1 mark each).
exam.tip: Steel is an alloy, not an element, so it does not count here.

exam.q: Describe the difference between a permanent magnet and an induced magnet.
model: A permanent magnet produces its own magnetic field all the time.
An induced magnet only becomes magnetic when placed in a magnetic field and loses (most of) its magnetism when removed.
exam.tip: Make one clear statement about each type, using the word field.

exam.q: Explain why a paper clip is always attracted, and never repelled, by either pole of a bar magnet.
model: The paper clip becomes an induced magnet in the magnet's field.
The end nearest the magnet becomes the opposite pole, so unlike poles attract.
exam.tip: Name the process (induced magnetism) and then use the pole rule.

exam.q: Draw the magnetic field pattern around a bar magnet.
model: Closed curved lines from one end of the magnet to the other, not crossing.
Arrows pointing from N to S.
Lines closer together near the poles.
exam.tip: At least four lines, arrows on every line, and no lines crossing or touching.

exam.q: Describe how a magnetic field's strength and direction change around a bar magnet.
model: The field is strongest at the poles.
The field gets weaker with increasing distance from the magnet.
The field direction is from N to S outside the magnet.
The direction changes continuously from point to point, following curved field lines (shown by a compass turning as it moves around).
exam.tip: Split your answer into strength (two points) and direction (two points).

exam.q: Describe how a plotting compass can be used to plot the magnetic field lines around a bar magnet.
model: Place the magnet on paper and put the compass near one pole.
Mark a dot where the north end of the needle points.
Move the compass so the tail of the needle is on the dot; mark the new position of the tip; repeat until the other pole.
Join the dots with a smooth line and add an arrow from N to S; repeat from different starting points.
exam.tip: Steps in order score best. Mention the arrow direction for the final mark.

exam.q: A student says iron filings are better than a compass for investigating a magnetic field. Evaluate this.
model: Iron filings quickly show the shape of the whole field pattern.
But they do not show the direction of the field, which a compass does.
exam.tip: Evaluate means give a point for and a point against.

exam.q: Explain how the behaviour of a magnetic compass provides evidence that the core of the Earth is magnetic.
model: A compass needle is a small magnet that lines up with a magnetic field.
With no magnets nearby, a compass always points in the same direction, north-south.
This happens everywhere on the Earth's surface, so there must be a magnetic field all around the Earth.
Compasses at different places point along lines matching the field pattern of a bar magnet.
The N end of a compass points to geographic north, so a magnetic south pole lies near the geographic North Pole.
This suggests the field is produced inside the Earth, so the core must be magnetic (made largely of iron and nickel).
exam.tip: Level of response question: build a logical chain from observation to conclusion and use magnetic field throughout.

exam.q: Two magnets are placed with a north pole facing a south pole. Describe the field in the gap between them.
model: Field lines are straight, parallel and evenly spaced (uniform field).
Direction from the N pole to the S pole.
exam.tip: Uniform is the key word: same strength and direction everywhere in the gap.

exam.q: Explain why soft iron is used for the core of an electromagnet rather than steel.
model: Soft iron is easily magnetised (becomes an induced magnet) when the current is on.
It loses its magnetism quickly when the current is switched off, so the magnet can be turned off.
exam.tip: Contrast with steel, which would stay magnetised.

worked.q: You are given three identical-looking metal bars, A, B and C. One is a permanent magnet, one is iron and one is aluminium. Using only the three bars, how can you identify each one?
steps: Bring the ends of the bars near each other in pairs.
Aluminium is not magnetic, so the bar that never feels any force with either other bar is aluminium.
The remaining two always attract each other at first, so attraction alone does not help.
Repulsion needs two magnets, so with only one magnet present neither pair will repel. A different test is needed.

Instead, use the middle of each bar: hold the end of bar X against the middle of bar Y. A magnet's field is weak at its middle, so if X is iron it is barely attracted by the middle of the magnet Y. If X is the magnet, its strong pole attracts the middle of the iron bar Y firmly.
So the bar whose end strongly attracts the middle of the other bar is the permanent magnet.
worked.ans: The bar with no force is aluminium. Of the other two, the one whose end strongly attracts the middle of the other is the magnet; the other is iron.

worked.q: Model answer: a compass is moved from the N pole of a bar magnet, around the side, to the S pole. Describe what the needle does and explain why.
steps: Near the N pole the field points straight away from N, so the compass needle points directly away from the magnet.
As the compass moves round the side, it follows the curved field line, so the needle turns gradually.
At the middle of the side the needle lies parallel to the magnet, pointing towards the S end.
Near the S pole the field points into S, so the needle points towards the magnet.
The needle turns because it is a small magnet: forces on its poles rotate it until it lines up with the field.
worked.ans: The needle turns steadily through about 180 degrees, always lying along the field line, with its N end pointing in the field direction from N to S.

phy_ocrb.2.9.summary: An electric current always produces a **magnetic field**. Around a **long straight wire** the field lines are **concentric circles** whose direction is given by the **right-hand grip rule**, and the field is stronger for a bigger current and closer to the wire. Winding the wire into a **solenoid** adds the fields of every turn, giving a strong, uniform field inside and a bar-magnet shaped field outside; adding a **soft iron core** makes an even stronger **electromagnet** that can be switched on and off. In a **loudspeaker** (triple), an alternating current in a coil sitting in a permanent magnet's field makes the coil and cone vibrate, producing sound.

core.h: A current produces a magnetic field
core.p: Whenever charge flows through a wire, a **magnetic field** is produced around it. This is called the **magnetic effect of a current**. Switch off the current and the field disappears; reverse the current and the field reverses.
bullets: Demonstration: place a plotting compass next to a wire. Switch on a large current: the needle **deflects**, showing a magnetic field.
Reverse the current: the needle swings the **opposite way**, so the field direction depends on the current direction.
Switch off: the needle returns to pointing north (Earth's field only).
This was first noticed by Oersted, and links electricity and magnetism: it is the basis of electromagnets, motors and loudspeakers.

callouts.p: A current in a wire produces a magnetic field around it. The direction of the field depends on the direction of the current.

core.h: Demonstrating the field around a straight wire
core.p: To see the field pattern, pass a straight vertical wire through a horizontal piece of card and connect it to a low-voltage supply that can give a large current.
bullets: Sprinkle **iron filings** on the card and tap it gently: the filings form **circles around the wire**.
Place several **plotting compasses** on the card in a circle around the wire: the needles point along the circles, showing the **direction**.
Reverse the current and all the compass needles turn round by 180 degrees.
Use a large current only briefly, because the wire gets hot.
Move the compasses further away: they are deflected less, because the field is weaker.

callouts.p: Large currents heat the wire. Switch on only while taking readings and use a low-voltage supply.

core.h: Field pattern of a long straight wire
core.p: The field lines around a straight current-carrying wire are **concentric circles** centred on the wire, in a plane at right angles to the wire.
bullets: The circles get **further apart** moving away from the wire, because the field gets **weaker with distance**.
The field is **stronger when the current is bigger**.
The field is **stronger closer to the wire**.
Seen end on, a **dot** means current coming **out of the page** towards you; a **cross** means current going **into the page**.
Current out of the page gives an **anticlockwise** field; current into the page gives a **clockwise** field.

callouts.p: Think of an arrow: you see its point (dot) as it flies towards you and its tail feathers (cross) as it flies away.

fig.cap: Field around a long straight wire, seen end-on. The field lines are concentric circles centred on the wire. Current coming out of the page (dot) gives an anticlockwise field; current into the page (cross) gives a clockwise field, as the right-hand grip rule predicts. The circles get further apart with distance because the field gets weaker.

core.p: The **right-hand grip rule** gives the direction of the magnetic field around a wire. Grip the wire with your **right hand** with your **thumb pointing in the direction of the (conventional) current**. Your **fingers curl in the direction of the field lines**.
bullets: Conventional current flows from + to minus around a circuit.
Use your right hand only: the left hand is for Fleming's motor rule.
Reverse the current and the field direction reverses.
The same rule works for a solenoid: curl your fingers round the coil in the direction of the current and your thumb points to the **north pole** end.

callouts.p: Point the right thumb in the direction of the current; the curled fingers show the direction of the magnetic field around the wire.

core.h: Factors affecting the field around a wire
core.p: The strength of the magnetic field around a straight wire depends on two things.
bullets: **Size of the current**: a larger current gives a stronger field.
**Distance from the wire**: the field gets weaker as you move further away.
The direction of the field depends only on the **direction of the current**.
In a diagram, a stronger field is shown by circles drawn closer together.

core.p: A **solenoid** is a long coil of wire. When current flows, the fields from all the individual turns **add together**. This is how a solenoid **enhances** (increases) the magnetic effect of the current.
bullets: Inside the solenoid the field lines are **straight, parallel and equally spaced**: the field is **strong and uniform**.
Outside, the field has the **same shape as a bar magnet's field**, with a north pole at one end and a south pole at the other.
Between neighbouring turns, the fields of the wires point in opposite directions and largely **cancel**; inside the coil they point the same way and **reinforce**.
Reversing the current swaps the N and S ends.
End rule: looking at one end, if the current flows **anticlockwise** that end is **N**; if **clockwise** it is **S**.

callouts.p: Every turn of the coil adds its field to the same region inside the coil, so the field inside is much stronger than around a single straight wire carrying the same current.

fig.cap: Field of a solenoid (long coil). Inside, the lines are straight, parallel and equally spaced: a strong, uniform field. Outside, the field has the same shape as a bar magnet. With current flowing down the front of each turn (red arrows), the right-hand grip rule puts the N pole at the right-hand end; seen from that end the current flows anticlockwise.

core.p: The spec asks how a solenoid arrangement enhances the magnetic effect. There are three main ways to increase the field strength of a solenoid.
bullets: Increase the **current** in the coil.
Increase the **number of turns** (wind the coil more tightly, more turns per unit length).
Put a **soft iron core** inside the coil: the iron becomes an induced magnet, and its field adds to the coil's field, making it much stronger.
Increasing the number of turns in the same length concentrates more of the field inside the coil.

callouts.p: More current, more turns, iron core: learn these as a list of three for electromagnet questions.

core.p: An **electromagnet** is a solenoid wrapped around a **soft iron core**. It is a magnet that can be **switched on and off** and whose strength can be changed by changing the current.
bullets: Soft iron is used because it is **easily magnetised** when the current flows and **loses its magnetism quickly** when the current stops.
Steel would stay magnetised and so could not be switched off properly.
Uses: scrap-yard cranes, electric bells, relays and circuit breakers, magnetic door locks, MRI scanners.
The strength can be adjusted by changing the current, unlike a permanent magnet.

core.p: A **moving-coil loudspeaker** turns electrical signals into sound. It uses the force on a current-carrying coil in a magnetic field (the motor effect).
bullets: A **permanent magnet** shaped so that there is a strong field in a narrow circular gap.
A light **coil of wire** sitting in the gap, so that its wire is at right angles to the magnetic field.
The coil is fixed to a **paper (or plastic) cone** that can move back and forth.
The coil is connected to an **amplifier** that supplies an **alternating current** with the same pattern as the sound.

fig.cap: Cross-section of a moving-coil loudspeaker. The coil sits in the gap of a permanent magnet and is fixed to a paper cone. Alternating current in the coil makes a force (the motor effect) that keeps changing direction, so the coil and cone vibrate back and forth (red double arrow) and push on the air, making sound waves.
