core.p: The loudspeaker works because a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field feels a **force**. With alternating current, the force keeps reversing.
bullets: An **alternating current** flows through the coil.
The coil is in the magnetic field of the permanent magnet, so a **force acts on the coil** (the motor effect).
When the current reverses, the **force reverses**, so the coil is pushed out and pulled in repeatedly.
The coil and the cone **vibrate** back and forth at the **same frequency as the alternating current**.
The cone pushes and pulls on the air, making **compressions and rarefactions**: a **sound wave** (longitudinal).
A **larger current** gives a larger force and bigger vibrations, so a **louder** sound (larger amplitude).
A **higher frequency** current gives a **higher pitch** sound.

callouts.p: The cone vibrates at the same frequency as the alternating current, so the sound produced has that frequency.

core.h: Headphones and the link to microphones
core.p: Headphones contain tiny loudspeakers that work in exactly the same way. A moving-coil microphone is built in the same way but works in reverse.
bullets: Loudspeaker: electrical signal in, sound out (uses the motor effect).
Microphone: sound in, electrical signal out (uses electromagnetic induction, covered separately).
In both, the coil must be light so it can follow rapid vibrations.

callouts.p: A loudspeaker needs a current supplied to it. Saying the loudspeaker induces a current is the microphone, not the speaker.

analogy.p: Imagine sticking a straight spoon vertically into water and stirring: the water swirls round in circles centred on the spoon, fastest close to the spoon and slower further away. The current is like the spoon's motion and the swirling water is like the circular magnetic field, stronger near the wire and weaker further out; stirring the other way reverses the swirl, just as reversing the current reverses the field. A solenoid is like a row of spoons all stirring together so their swirls add up in the middle. The analogy breaks down because nothing actually flows round a magnetic field line, and the field exists in a vacuum with no material to swirl.

terms.d: A current in a conductor produces a magnetic field around it.
Circles with the same centre; the shape of the field lines around a straight wire.
Thumb in the direction of the current; curled fingers give the direction of the magnetic field.
Current direction taken as from the positive terminal to the negative terminal around a circuit.
A long coil of wire; with a current it produces a field like a bar magnet outside and a uniform field inside.
A field of the same strength and direction everywhere, shown by straight, parallel, equally spaced lines.
A coil of wire around a soft iron core that is a magnet only while a current flows.
Iron inside a coil that is easily magnetised and demagnetised, greatly increasing the field strength.
The number of loops of wire in a coil; more turns give a stronger field.
A small compass used to show the direction of a magnetic field at a point.
The force on a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field.
A device that uses the motor effect on a coil carrying alternating current to make a cone vibrate and produce sound.
A current that repeatedly reverses direction.
A device that supplies a larger version of an electrical signal to a loudspeaker.
Regions of higher and lower air pressure in a sound wave.

mistakes.w: The field lines around a wire go along the wire.
mistakes.r: The field lines are concentric circles around the wire, at right angles to it.

mistakes.w: The field around a wire is the same strength everywhere.
mistakes.r: The field is stronger closer to the wire and for a larger current; the circles get further apart with distance.

mistakes.w: Use the left hand to find the field direction around a wire.
mistakes.r: Use the right-hand grip rule: thumb along the current, fingers give the field.

mistakes.w: The field inside a solenoid is weak and curved.
mistakes.r: Inside a solenoid the field is strong and uniform: straight, parallel, equally spaced lines.

mistakes.w: Use a steel core to make a stronger electromagnet that switches off.
mistakes.r: Use soft iron, which magnetises easily and loses its magnetism when the current is switched off; steel stays magnetised.

mistakes.w: Make the electromagnet stronger by using a bigger coil.
mistakes.r: Increase the current, increase the number of turns, or add a soft iron core.

mistakes.w: In a loudspeaker the magnet vibrates.
mistakes.r: The coil (and the cone fixed to it) vibrates; the permanent magnet stays still.

mistakes.w: The loudspeaker produces a current from sound.
mistakes.r: That is a microphone. A loudspeaker uses an alternating current to produce a force that makes the cone vibrate.

mistakes.w: A loudspeaker works with direct current.
mistakes.r: It needs alternating current so the force keeps reversing and the cone vibrates back and forth.

exam.q: Describe the shape of the magnetic field around a long straight current-carrying wire.
model: Concentric circles around the wire (centred on the wire).
Further apart (weaker) further from the wire.
exam.tip: Concentric is the key word.

exam.q: State two factors that affect the strength of the magnetic field at a point near a straight wire.
model: Size of the current.
Distance from the wire.
exam.tip: Say which way: bigger current gives a stronger field; greater distance gives a weaker field.

exam.q: Describe an experiment to show that a current-carrying wire produces a magnetic field.
model: Pass a vertical wire through a horizontal card and connect it to a d.c. supply.
Place plotting compasses (or iron filings) on the card around the wire.
Switch on: the compasses point in circles around the wire (filings form circles).
Reverse the current: the compass needles reverse direction, showing the field depends on the current direction.
exam.tip: Include an observation as well as the method; mention reversing the current for the direction mark.

exam.q: State the rule used to find the direction of the magnetic field around a wire.
model: Right-hand grip rule: thumb points along the current, fingers curl in the direction of the field.
exam.tip: Naming the rule may get the mark, but describing it is safer.

exam.q: Describe the magnetic field inside and outside a solenoid carrying a current.
model: Inside: strong and uniform (straight, parallel, equally spaced lines).
Outside: same shape as the field of a bar magnet.
It has a N pole at one end and a S pole at the other, which swap if the current is reversed.
exam.tip: Inside and outside both need describing for full marks.

exam.q: Explain how a solenoid arrangement can enhance the magnetic effect of a current.
model: Each turn of the coil produces its own magnetic field.
Inside the coil the fields from all the turns point the same way and add together.
So the field inside is much stronger than around a single wire (and uniform).
Adding more turns, a larger current or a soft iron core increases it further.
exam.tip: Explain adding together of fields, then list ways to make it stronger.

exam.q: Give two reasons why soft iron is used for the core of an electromagnet.
model: It is easily magnetised, making the field much stronger.
It loses its magnetism when the current is switched off.
exam.tip: Both reasons are about induced magnetism.

exam.q: A crane uses an electromagnet to lift scrap steel. Suggest one advantage of using an electromagnet rather than a permanent magnet.
model: It can be switched off to drop the steel (or its strength can be changed).
exam.tip: Link the advantage to the use in the question.

exam.q: Explain how a loudspeaker produces sound.
model: An alternating current from the amplifier flows in the coil.
The coil is in the magnetic field of a permanent magnet.
A force acts on the coil because of the motor effect (current at right angles to the field).
The current keeps reversing, so the force keeps reversing direction.
The coil and attached cone vibrate back and forth at the frequency of the current.
The cone makes the air vibrate, producing compressions and rarefactions: a sound wave of the same frequency.
exam.tip: Level of response question: give a clear sequence from current to force to vibration to sound.

exam.q: State the effect on the sound from a loudspeaker of increasing the frequency of the alternating current.
model: The pitch of the sound increases (higher frequency sound).
exam.tip: Frequency links to pitch; amplitude links to loudness.

exam.q: Explain why the sound from a loudspeaker gets louder when the current is increased.
model: A larger current gives a larger force on the coil.
So the cone vibrates with a larger amplitude, giving a louder sound.
exam.tip: Force first, then amplitude, then loudness.

worked.q: A vertical wire carries current upwards through a horizontal card. Seen from above, which way do the field lines go? A compass is placed due east of the wire. Which way does its N end point?
steps: Seen from above, current coming up through the card is coming out of the page towards you (a dot).
Right-hand grip rule: thumb up (towards you), fingers curl anticlockwise as seen from above.
Take north as the top of the page and east to the right. To the east of the wire, an anticlockwise circle is moving upwards on the page.
So the field there points north, and the compass N end points north (ignoring the Earth's field).
worked.ans: The field lines are anticlockwise circles seen from above; at the point due east of the wire the compass N end points north.

worked.q: A solenoid is connected so that, looking at its left-hand end, the current flows clockwise. Which end is the north pole? What two changes would make the field stronger without changing the polarity?
steps: End rule: clockwise current seen at an end means that end is a south pole.
So the left-hand end is S and the right-hand end is N.
Check with the right-hand grip rule: curl fingers with the current, thumb points to the right, so N is on the right.
To make it stronger without reversing it: increase the current (same direction), and add more turns or a soft iron core.
worked.ans: The right-hand end is N. Increase the current in the same direction and add more turns or a soft iron core.
